evidenceRatingScale: 1-5 stars informed by Schoenfeld hypertrophy literature, Stronger By Science syntheses, Renaissance Periodization volume guidance, and ExRx biomechanics. 5 = top-tier compound with strong evidence. 1 = niche or weak evidence.

exercises.name: Barbell Bench Press
exercises.cue: Tuck elbows ~45° from torso, drive feet into floor, bar to lower sternum.
exercises.description: The classic chest builder. You lie on a flat bench and press a loaded barbell from your chest to arm's length. It trains the chest, the front of your shoulders, and the back of your arms all at once, which is why it's the most-studied chest exercise on the planet.
steps: Lie flat on the bench so your eyes are directly under the bar.
Set your feet flat on the floor and squeeze your shoulder blades together and down into the bench.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width with wrists stacked over elbows.
Unrack the bar and hold it over your shoulders with arms straight.
Lower the bar slowly to your lower chest, keeping elbows tucked at about 45° from your torso.
Press the bar back up by pushing your chest into the bar, exhaling as you lock out.
Reset your breath and brace before the next rep.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Imagine pushing the bench down through the floor with your chest, not just pushing the bar up.
commonMistakes: Flaring elbows out to 90°: lets the shoulder take over and risks injury. Tuck them to 45°.
Bouncing the bar off the chest: cheats the hardest part of the rep. Lower under control and pause briefly.
Lifting the hips off the bench: turns it into a decline press. Keep glutes glued down.
tips: Use a spotter for working sets above 80% of your max — or use the Smith machine variant in this catalog.
If your wrists hurt, stack them straight over the elbows instead of letting them bend back.

exercises.name: Incline Barbell Bench Press
exercises.cue: Set bench to ~30°; bar touches upper chest; biases clavicular pec.
exercises.description: A bench press done on an inclined bench that shifts the work to the upper portion of your chest — the part right below your collarbone. It also pulls in more front-shoulder than a flat press, so it doubles as a press that fills out the top of the chest where flat bench tends to underwork.
steps: Set the bench to roughly 30 degrees — any steeper and it becomes mostly a shoulder press.
Lie back and pull your shoulder blades down and together against the bench.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width and unrack it directly over your upper chest.
Lower the bar in a controlled line until it lightly touches your upper chest, just below the collarbone.
Press up and slightly back so the bar finishes over your shoulders, not your face.
Lock out without slamming, then reset for the next rep.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the top slice of your chest, just under the collarbone, pulling the bar down and pushing it back up.
commonMistakes: Setting the bench too steep (45°+): turns it into a shoulder press. Stick to 30°.
Letting the bar drift toward the chin: dumps load onto the shoulders. Keep it tracking over the upper chest.
Losing the upper-back arch: kills your power base. Stay tight and pinned to the bench.
tips: If your gym only has fixed incline benches at 45°, stack a folded towel under one end to soften the angle.
Lighter loads than flat bench — start around 70% of your flat press.

exercises.name: Decline Bench Press
exercises.cue: Slight decline; bar to lower chest; biases lower pec fibers.
exercises.description: A bench press done with your head lower than your hips. The angle biases the lower fibers of the chest and takes the front shoulders out of the lift. The short range of motion lets most people press more weight here than on flat bench.
steps: Hook your feet under the pads and lie back on the decline bench.
Pull your shoulder blades together and brace your core.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width and unrack it with help if possible.
Lower the bar slowly to your lower chest, keeping elbows tucked.
Press the bar back up over your shoulders, exhaling at lockout.
Re-rack carefully — getting up from a decline takes some effort.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the lower edge of your chest, near the bottom of your sternum, doing the pressing.
commonMistakes: Pressing without a spotter: getting stuck under the bar on a decline is dangerous. Use a spotter or Smith.
Bouncing the bar: shortens range of motion and risks rib injury. Control the lower.
Flaring elbows wide: same chest-vs-shoulder problem as flat bench. Keep them in.
tips: Many Indian gyms lack a dedicated decline bench — a Smith machine with the bench at a slight decline works fine.
Skip this if flat bench already feels great. The chest works as one muscle and decline is the most replaceable angle.

exercises.name: Dumbbell Bench Press
exercises.cue: Stretch deeper than barbell; press dumbbells together at top.
exercises.description: Same lift as a bench press, but with a dumbbell in each hand. Because the dumbbells can travel below the chest line and your hands aren't fixed to a bar, you get a deeper stretch and each side has to work independently — which fixes left/right strength imbalances over time.
steps: Sit on the bench with a dumbbell on each thigh, then kick them up to your shoulders as you lie back.
Plant your feet and pull your shoulder blades together.
Press the dumbbells up so they're directly over your shoulders, palms facing your feet.
Lower the dumbbells slowly until your elbows drop just below the bench line.
Press back up and slightly inward so the dumbbells almost touch at the top.
After the last rep, sit up by pulling the dumbbells back to your thighs.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: At the bottom, feel the chest stretching wide; at the top, feel the chest squeezing the dumbbells together.
commonMistakes: Touching the dumbbells together hard at the top: kills tension. Stop just before they touch and squeeze.
Letting the dumbbells drift apart at the bottom: loads the shoulders. Keep them over the elbows.
Bad setup that drops a dumbbell on the floor: always kick them up from your thighs, never lift from the floor.
tips: Many Indian gyms cap dumbbells at 40–50 kg — when you outgrow them, switch to barbell or Smith for working sets.
Slow the lowering phase to 3 seconds for an extra growth stimulus without going heavier.

exercises.name: Incline Dumbbell Press
exercises.cue: 30° bench; lower until elbows are slightly below torso line.
exercises.description: An incline press done with dumbbells. You get the upper-chest bias of the incline angle plus the deeper stretch and independent arm work of dumbbells. For most lifters this is the single best exercise for filling out the top of the chest.
steps: Set the bench to roughly 30 degrees.
Sit with a dumbbell on each thigh, then kick them up as you lie back.
Pull your shoulder blades down and together, then press the dumbbells over your shoulders.
Lower them slowly until your elbows are slightly below your torso line — you should feel a real stretch.
Press up and slightly inward, stopping just before the dumbbells touch.
Pull the dumbbells back to your thighs to dismount safely.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the upper chest stretch open at the bottom like the muscle is yawning, then squeeze it tight at the top.
commonMistakes: Using too steep an incline (45°+): the shoulders steal the work. Keep it at 30°.
Crashing the dumbbells together at lockout: dumps tension. Stop short.
Letting the elbows flare wide at the bottom: stresses the shoulder. Keep them at ~45°.
tips: On the last rep, hold the bottom stretch for a 2-second count — incline dumbbells respond hard to long stretches.
If the gym's adjustable benches only lock at 45°, prop the back of a flat bench on a step or plate.

exercises.name: Machine Chest Press
exercises.cue: Sit upright; press without flaring elbows wide; controlled eccentric.
exercises.description: A seated chest press on a plate-loaded or selectorized machine. The fixed path means you don't need to balance the weight, so you can really focus on pushing the chest hard. Great for beginners learning to press and for finishers after free-weight work.
steps: Adjust the seat so the handles line up with the middle of your chest.
Sit tall and pull your shoulder blades down and back into the pad.
Grip the handles and lift your chest into the press position.
Press the handles forward in a controlled arc until your arms are almost straight.
Lower slowly until you feel a stretch across the chest — don't slam the stack.
After the last rep, let the weight settle back to the start before standing up.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Picture your hands trying to meet in front of your chest — drive with the chest, not the arms.
commonMistakes: Setting the seat too low or too high: handles should hit mid-chest, not face or belly.
Locking elbows hard at the top: dumps tension off the chest. Stop just before lockout.
Banging the stack on the way down: cheats the eccentric. Lower under control.
tips: If your gym has a converging chest press (handles arc inward), use it — it gives a better chest squeeze than parallel-path machines.
This is the safest place to push close to failure since you can't get pinned.

exercises.name: Smith Machine Bench Press
exercises.cue: Fixed bar path; good for high-rep work or training without a spotter.
exercises.description: A bench press performed on a Smith machine, where the bar slides along fixed rails. You lose the balance demand of a free barbell, but you gain safety — you can rack the bar at any height by twisting your wrists. Useful when training alone or when chasing chest fatigue with no risk of getting pinned.
steps: Position a flat bench under the Smith bar so the bar lines up with your lower chest.
Lie down, plant your feet, and squeeze your shoulder blades together.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width, then twist your wrists forward to unrack.
Lower the bar to your lower chest, keeping elbows tucked at about 45°.
Press back up and stop just shy of lockout.
After your last rep, twist your wrists back to re-rack the bar.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Since the bar can't go anywhere, pour all your attention into squeezing the chest on every inch of the press.
commonMistakes: Setting up too far up or down the bench: bar path no longer hits your lower chest. Reposition the bench.
Forgetting how the hooks rotate: practice the twist-to-rack motion before adding weight.
Treating it like a free bench and not exploring deeper ROM: take advantage of the safety and stretch deeper.
tips: The Smith machine in most Indian gyms tilts slightly — angled rails mean you should pick a bench position that matches the bar's natural travel, not the gym's marked spots.
This is the best place to do drop sets and long high-rep finishers on chest day.

exercises.name: Dip (Chest Bias)
exercises.cue: Lean torso forward ~30° throughout; chest stretches at the bottom.
exercises.description: A bodyweight press done on parallel bars where you lower and lift your whole body. Leaning forward shifts the work onto the lower and outer chest — many lifters find this their favorite chest stretcher. You can add load with a dip belt as you get stronger.
steps: Grip the parallel bars and press up to a straight-arm support position.
Cross your ankles behind you and tilt your torso forward about 30 degrees.
Keep that forward lean and lower yourself until your shoulders drop just below your elbows.
Stop at the point where you feel a strong chest stretch.
Press back up by squeezing the chest, keeping the forward lean the whole way.
Stop just short of full elbow lockout to keep tension on the chest.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: At the bottom, feel like your chest is being pulled apart; on the press, squeeze the bars together with your chest.
commonMistakes: Going upright instead of leaning forward: turns it into a tricep dip. Maintain a 30° lean.
Dropping too deep without shoulder mobility: causes shoulder pain. Stop where the chest stretch starts, not where pain does.
Bouncing at the bottom: risky for the shoulders. Pause briefly, then press.
tips: If your gym's dip station rocks or wobbles, use the assisted pull-up machine's dip handles instead.
Add load with a dip belt or a dumbbell between your feet once you can do 12 clean bodyweight reps.

exercises.name: Push-Up
exercises.cue: Hands under shoulders; full body line; lower chest to within an inch of floor.
exercises.description: The original chest exercise. You hold a plank position and lower your chest to the floor, then press back up. It hits the chest, triceps, and front shoulders, and it also forces your core to hold a solid line — making it a sneaky full-body movement.
steps: Place your hands on the floor slightly wider than shoulder-width, fingers spread.
Extend your legs back, feet together, body in a straight line from heels to head.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes so your hips don't sag.
Lower your body slowly until your chest is about an inch off the floor.
Keep elbows at roughly 45° from your torso — not flared out wide.
Press back up by pushing the floor away, stopping just shy of locked elbows.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Imagine you're trying to push the floor down rather than push your body up — keep the chest doing the work.
commonMistakes: Sagging hips: turns it into a back exercise. Squeeze glutes and core to keep a straight line.
Flaring elbows out wide: stresses the shoulders. Tuck to 45°.
Cutting depth: chest must come within an inch of the floor or it's a half rep.
tips: If full push-ups are too hard, put your hands on a bench — easier angle, still trains the same pattern.
Once 20+ reps feel easy, slow down the lowering phase to 4 seconds before adding load with a plate on the back.

exercises.name: Cable Fly
exercises.cue: Slight constant elbow bend; arc hands together at sternum height.
exercises.description: A pure chest squeeze. Standing in the middle of a cable crossover with handles in each hand, you arc your arms inward as if hugging a tree. The cables keep tension on the chest at every point, including the top where dumbbells lose it.
steps: Set both cable pulleys to roughly chest height.
Stand in the middle, grab a handle in each hand, and step forward to load the cables.
Stand with a slight forward lean and feet split for balance.
Keep a soft, fixed bend in your elbows — don't let them straighten or close.
Arc your hands together in front of your sternum, squeezing the chest hard at the meeting point.
Return slowly with control, letting the cables stretch the chest wide before the next rep.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel like you're hugging a huge tree — the chest pulls your hands toward each other, the arms are just hooks.
commonMistakes: Bending and straightening the elbows: turns it into a press. Keep elbow angle locked.
Standing too close to the cables: kills the stretch. Step out until you feel tension at the start.
Pulling the handles too low or too high: aim for sternum height for the best chest line.
tips: Try high-to-low (handles at top) for lower chest bias and low-to-high for upper chest bias.
Squeeze and hold for a one-count at the inside position — it's where most of the growth signal is.

exercises.name: Dumbbell Fly
exercises.cue: Soft elbow bend; stretch wide, hug-a-tree at top; don't muscle with shoulders.
exercises.description: A chest isolation move done lying on a flat bench with a dumbbell in each hand. You arc the weights out to the sides and back together over your chest. The exercise gets its growth power from the deep stretch at the bottom of the arc.
steps: Sit on a flat bench with a dumbbell on each thigh and kick them up as you lie back.
Press the dumbbells up over your chest with a slight bend in the elbows.
Lock that elbow bend in — it should not change for the whole set.
Lower the dumbbells out to your sides in a wide arc until you feel a deep chest stretch.
Reverse the arc by squeezing the chest, bringing the dumbbells back together over your chest.
Stop just before the dumbbells touch to keep tension, then repeat.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel like you're hugging a tree — wide open at the bottom, squeezing the chest at the top.
commonMistakes: Letting elbows fully straighten: shifts load onto the joint. Keep that soft bend locked.
Going too heavy and turning it into a press: defeats the isolation. Drop the weight.
Dropping below shoulder level too fast: risks tearing the chest. Lower under control.
tips: Cable flies have more constant tension — save dumbbell flies for when you want the deep stretch position.
Stay light, especially when learning. 30% of your bench press weight is plenty to start.

exercises.name: Pec Deck
exercises.cue: Forearms flat on pads; squeeze chest, not shoulders; pause at peak.
exercises.description: A seated machine that mimics a chest fly. You press your forearms or grip handles to bring them together in front of your chest. The machine gives constant tension and removes balance demands, so you can focus 100 percent on squeezing the chest.
steps: Adjust the seat so the pads or handles line up with the middle of your chest.
Sit tall with your back firmly against the pad.
Place your forearms or hands on the pads with elbows bent to about 90 degrees.
Pull your arms together by squeezing the chest, not pulling with the shoulders.
Pause and hard squeeze when your arms meet in the middle.
Return slowly to feel a deep chest stretch before the next rep.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Forget the arms — pretend your chest muscles are clapping their hands in front of you.
commonMistakes: Shrugging shoulders during the squeeze: traps take over. Keep shoulders pinned down.
Pulling too far behind you on the way back: shoulder strain. Stop where you feel a stretch, not pain.
Rushing the reps: kills the squeeze. Pause at peak for one full count.
tips: Some Indian gyms only have the forearm-pad style — check that your forearms sit fully flat for a clean line of force.
Great finisher after pressing — go light and chase the pump.

exercises.name: Dumbbell Pullover
exercises.cue: Lie across bench; arc dumbbell over and behind head; deep ribcage stretch.
exercises.description: An old-school exercise where you lie across a bench and arc a single dumbbell from over your chest to behind your head. It stretches the chest and lats hard at the bottom — uncommon to find in modern programs but a great way to open up the ribcage and finish a chest workout.
steps: Place a dumbbell on the end of a flat bench.
Lie across the bench with just your upper back on it, feet planted wide for balance.
Pick up the dumbbell with both hands cupped around the top plate and press it over your chest.
Keep a slight, fixed bend in your elbows.
Arc the dumbbell back and over your head, lowering until you feel a deep stretch across the chest and lats.
Pull the dumbbell back over your chest in the same arc, squeezing the chest at the top.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel your ribcage opening up wide at the bottom — like taking the biggest possible breath.
commonMistakes: Bending the elbows to lift more weight: turns it into a tricep exercise. Lock the elbow bend.
Dropping the hips: misaligns the spine. Keep hips low but level.
Going too heavy and tearing through the shoulders: this is a stretch exercise, not a strength move.
tips: Hold the bottom stretch position for a 2-count — the stretch is where the gains live.
If you can't find a heavy dumbbell that's safe to hold by one end, use two hands clasped around the handle of a kettlebell instead.

exercises.name: Barbell Deadlift (Conventional)
exercises.cue: Bar over mid-foot; brace hard; push the floor away, don't yank with the back.
exercises.description: Pick a heavy loaded barbell up off the floor and stand up with it. That's a deadlift. It's the most complete strength exercise in existence — your entire back, glutes, hamstrings, and grip all work as one. Done well it builds raw strength; done poorly it's the fastest way to a tweaked back, so respect the technique.
steps: Stand with feet hip-width apart and the bar over the middle of your feet, almost touching your shins.
Hinge down and grip the bar just outside your knees with both hands.
Pull yourself down to the bar — chest up, back flat, shoulders just in front of the bar.
Take a big breath, brace your core hard, and 'pull the slack' out of the bar.
Push the floor away with your legs while keeping the bar dragging up your shins.
Stand fully upright, squeeze the glutes, and stop — no lean back.
Lower the bar by hinging at the hips first, then bending the knees once it passes them.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel like you're pushing the earth down with your feet — the bar comes up because the floor goes down.
commonMistakes: Rounding the lower back: highest injury risk in the gym. Keep the back flat or naturally arched.
Bar drifting away from the shins: doubles the load on your back. Keep it brushing your legs the whole way.
Hyperextending at the top: stresses the lower back. Stand tall, don't lean back.
tips: Use mixed grip (one over, one under) or chalk once your grip starts giving out before your back does.
Take 2–3 minutes rest between heavy sets — deadlifts are taxing, not a circuit move.
Skip this entirely on weeks when your lower back feels tight.

exercises.name: Pull-Up
exercises.cue: Pull elbows down to ribs; lead with chest, not chin.
exercises.description: Hang from a bar with palms facing away and pull yourself up until your chin clears it. The pull-up is the king of back exercises and one of the strongest indicators of relative strength. Every part of your back works, your biceps assist, and your grip gets brutally trained as a bonus.
steps: Reach up and grip the pull-up bar slightly wider than shoulder-width with palms facing away.
Hang with arms fully straight and shoulders pulled down (no shrug).
Take a breath and brace your core, legs slightly forward or crossed behind you.
Pull yourself up by driving your elbows down toward your ribs.
Continue until your chin clears the bar — chest leads, don't crane your neck.
Lower slowly back to a full hang, control the descent for 2 seconds.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Imagine your elbows trying to touch your back pockets — the bar comes to you because your elbows are driving down.
commonMistakes: Kipping (swinging the legs to cheat the rep): trains nothing well. Stay still and strict.
Half-reps that never reach a full hang: shortchanges the lats. Always go to straight arms.
Craning the neck to clear the chin: stresses the spine. Pull your chest up instead.
tips: Can't do one yet? Use the assisted pull-up machine in this catalog or do slow eccentrics by jumping up and lowering for 5+ seconds.
Once you can do 8 strict reps, add load with a dip belt for new growth.

exercises.name: Chin-Up
exercises.cue: Underhand grip, shoulder width; full hang to chest-to-bar.
exercises.description: A pull-up with your palms facing you instead of away. The underhand grip pulls the biceps deeper into the movement, which makes chin-ups easier than pull-ups for most people and a great way to train back and biceps together when time is tight.
steps: Grip the bar shoulder-width apart with palms facing you.
Hang fully with arms straight and shoulders pulled down.
Brace your core and cross your ankles behind you.
Pull up by driving elbows down and slightly back.
Continue until your chin clears the bar or your collarbone touches it.
Lower slowly back to a full hang before the next rep.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel both the back and the biceps cranking you upward — like a heavy biceps curl that lifts your whole body.
commonMistakes: Not going to a full hang: cheats the stretch. Straighten the arms each rep.
Pulling with just the arms and neglecting the back: keep elbows driving down, not just bending.
Swinging the legs: trains momentum, not strength. Stay still.
tips: Chin-ups are usually 2–3 reps stronger than pull-ups — use them when you want more total reps.
If your elbow tendons get cranky, switch to neutral-grip handles for a couple weeks.

exercises.name: Lat Pulldown
exercises.cue: Pull bar to upper chest; drive elbows down, not back.
exercises.description: Seated at a cable station, you pull a wide bar down from overhead to your upper chest. It trains the same lat-pulling pattern as a pull-up but lets you dial in the load — perfect for beginners building up to bodyweight pull-ups and for adding back volume at any level.
steps: Set the thigh pad so it locks you firmly into the seat.
Stand, grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width, then sit down with the bar overhead.
Lean back about 15 degrees and pull your shoulder blades down before the arms move.
Pull the bar down to your upper chest by driving elbows down and slightly back.
Squeeze the lats hard at the bottom for a one-count.
Let the bar travel back up under control to a full overhead stretch — no shrug.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Picture your elbows trying to drive down into your back pockets — the bar is just a handle on your elbows.
commonMistakes: Pulling behind the neck: stresses the shoulders. Always pull to the upper chest in front.
Leaning way back to grind out reps: turns it into a row. Keep lean to ~15°.
Shrugging at the top: hits traps instead of lats. Pull shoulders down before pulling the bar.
tips: Mix grip widths over a training cycle — slightly wider for upper lats, shoulder-width for thicker mid-back.
If your gym's lat pulldown uses a too-thick bar, swap it for a straight bar attachment or use a wider rope.

exercises.name: Barbell Row (Bent-Over)
exercises.cue: Hinge to ~45°; pull bar to lower ribs; control the lower more than the lift.
exercises.description: A hinged-over barbell pull. You bend at the hips, hold the bar with arms long, and row it into your lower ribs. It builds thick mid-back, lats, and a stronger deadlift in one move. Holding the hinge is the hard part — once you get that, it's gold.
steps: Stand with feet hip-width apart, bar over mid-foot.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width, palms down.
Push your hips back and lower your torso to about 45 degrees with a flat back.
Let arms hang straight and pull your shoulder blades down.
Row the bar to your lower ribs by driving elbows up and back.
Squeeze your mid-back hard at the top, then lower slowly to arms-straight.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Try to crush a pencil between your shoulder blades when the bar touches your ribs.
commonMistakes: Rounding the back to lift more: injury risk. Drop the weight and stay flat.
Standing up too tall during the pull: turns it into a shrug. Stay hinged.
Pulling to the chest: hits rear delts instead of mid-back. Row to lower ribs.
tips: Underhand grip variation (palms up) lets you stay more upright and trains the lats harder — rotate it in.
Use straps once your grip fails before your back does, especially above 80 kg.

exercises.name: Pendlay Row
exercises.cue: Reset bar on floor each rep; explosive pull, dead stop, flat back.
exercises.description: A strict version of the barbell row, named after coach Glenn Pendlay. The bar starts on the floor each rep, you stay hinged at 90 degrees, and you pull the bar explosively to your chest. The dead stop kills momentum, which forces the back to do all the work.
steps: Stand with feet hip-width and bar over mid-foot.
Grip the bar wider than shoulder-width and hinge your torso to nearly parallel with the floor.
Brace hard with a flat back — torso angle stays here for every rep.
Row the bar explosively up to your lower chest.
Lower the bar all the way back to the floor and let it settle for a beat.
Reset your breath and brace, then pull again — no bouncing.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Imagine yanking the bar through the ceiling with your back, then setting a glass of water down on the floor.
commonMistakes: Letting the torso rise as you row: kills the strict bias. Stay hinged.
Bouncing the bar off the floor: defeats the dead stop. Pause for one beat.
Rounding the back at the bottom: pull yourself into position before each rep.
tips: Start lighter than your regular row — the strict torso position is much harder.
Save this for technique-focused days when you can keep form perfect.

exercises.name: Seated Cable Row
exercises.cue: Tall chest; pull handle to belly button; squeeze mid-back at end.
exercises.description: Sit at a cable row station with feet on the platform, knees slightly bent, and pull a handle into your stomach. The seated position takes the low back out of the equation, so all you have to think about is squeezing the mid-back hard.
steps: Sit on the bench with feet braced on the platform, knees slightly bent.
Grip the handle, sit tall, and lean back about 10 degrees.
Pull your shoulder blades down before the elbows move.
Row the handle into your belly button, driving elbows back and squeezing the mid-back.
Pause and squeeze for a one-count.
Let the handle return slowly, arms fully extended at the front — but don't let the torso lurch forward.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Try to crush a tennis ball between your shoulder blades at the back of every rep.
commonMistakes: Rocking the torso to swing the weight: turns it into momentum work. Lock the torso.
Letting the shoulders shrug up: traps take over. Keep shoulders down.
Pulling too high to the chest: shifts to rear delts. Pull to belly button.
tips: Swap attachments often — V-handle for lats, wide bar for mid-back, rope for rear delts.
Pause for a full second at the squeeze — the back grows from being held in the contracted position.

exercises.name: Single-Arm Dumbbell Row
exercises.cue: One knee on bench; pull dumbbell to hip, not chest; flat back throughout.
exercises.description: A single-arm row with one knee and one hand braced on a bench. You hang a dumbbell from the other arm and row it up to your hip. Excellent for fixing left-right back imbalances and for getting a longer range of motion than barbell rows.
steps: Place one knee and the same-side hand on a flat bench.
Plant the other foot on the floor, slightly back for balance.
Pick up a dumbbell in your free hand and let it hang under your shoulder.
Keep your back flat and parallel with the floor.
Row the dumbbell up to your hip, driving the elbow back and squeezing the lat.
Lower under control to a long-arm stretch before the next rep.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Pretend you're starting a lawnmower — pull the elbow back hard toward your hip, not your shoulder.
commonMistakes: Twisting the torso to add range: trains rotation, not the back. Keep the torso square.
Pulling to the armpit: turns it into a rear-delt move. Row to the hip.
Going too heavy and yanking with the body: drop the weight and feel the lat working.
tips: Slow the lowering phase to a 3-count for extra growth without going heavier.
Pair with a wide-grip pulldown — single-arm rows hit the lats from a different angle and complement perfectly.

exercises.name: T-Bar Row
exercises.cue: Chest supported when possible; pull handle to lower chest.
exercises.description: A row done with a barbell anchored to the floor at one end, with weight plates loaded on the other. You straddle the bar and pull a V-handle into your chest. The angle and grip make it feel friendlier on the lower back than a bent-over row while still hitting heavy mid-back work.
steps: Load the bar and stand over it with feet shoulder-width apart.
Hinge your torso to about 45 degrees with a flat back.
Attach a V-handle under the bar and grip it with both hands.
Stand up to lift the bar and let it hang at arms' length.
Row the handle up to your lower chest, driving elbows back.
Lower slowly until arms are straight, keeping torso hinged.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the mid-back muscles between your shoulder blades pulling the handle in toward your ribcage.
commonMistakes: Standing up during the pull: turns it into a deadlift. Stay hinged.
Rounding the back: the hinged position with weight is unforgiving. Keep the back flat.
Letting the bar drag on the ground between reps: kills tension. Hover an inch off the floor.
tips: If your gym has a chest-supported T-bar machine (the kind with a pad), use it — it removes lower-back fatigue entirely.
For Indian gyms without a T-bar landmine, wedge one end of a barbell into a corner with a folded towel to protect the wall.

exercises.name: Inverted Row
exercises.cue: Body in straight line; pull chest to bar; pause briefly.
exercises.description: An upside-down push-up for the back. You set a bar at hip height, hang underneath it, and pull your chest up to the bar. It's perfect for beginners building toward pull-ups and for adding back volume at home or with limited equipment.
steps: Set a barbell in a rack or use a Smith bar at hip height.
Lie under the bar and grip it slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Hang with arms straight, body in a straight line from heels to head.
Squeeze glutes and core so your hips don't sag.
Pull your chest up to the bar by driving elbows back and squeezing the mid-back.
Lower slowly back to a long-arm hang and repeat.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel like you're rowing a boat with your chest leading — back muscles squeeze, arms just bend.
commonMistakes: Sagging hips: turns it into a strange ab move. Squeeze glutes the whole set.
Half-reps that don't reach the bar: shortchanges the back. Touch chest to bar each time.
Bar too high or too low: bar at hip height is the sweet spot. Adjust the rack.
tips: Make it harder by elevating your feet on a bench, or easier by bending your knees more.
Great choice for travel or home days — only needs a bar at hip height.

exercises.name: Machine Row (Chest-Supported)
exercises.cue: Chest pad firm; lead with elbows, finish with squeeze; great for low-back days.
exercises.description: A row done seated against a chest pad on a plate-loaded or selectorized machine. The pad takes the lower back completely out of the lift, so you can push the back hard without worrying about form drift. Ideal for high-rep finishers and for days your back feels tired.
steps: Adjust the seat so the handles line up with the middle of your chest.
Sit with your chest pressed firmly against the pad.
Grip the handles and pull your shoulder blades down to start the rep.
Row the handles back by driving your elbows behind you.
Squeeze the mid-back hard at the end position.
Let the handles return slowly to a long-arm stretch before the next rep.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Picture pulling your elbows past your ribs — drive the elbows, the hands are just hooks.
commonMistakes: Pulling the chest off the pad: defeats the support. Keep chest glued to it.
Going too heavy and using the shoulders to shrug: stay on the back, not the traps.
Stopping short of full arm extension: skip the stretch and you skip the growth signal.
tips: Use a neutral grip (palms facing each other) for lats, overhand wide grip for mid-back.
This is the safest row to push close to failure — great spot for the last working set.

exercises.name: Straight-Arm Pulldown
exercises.cue: Soft elbows; arc bar to thighs; feel lats stretch and contract.
exercises.description: A lat isolation done at the cable station. You stand a step back from the stack and arc a bar or rope down from overhead to your thighs with nearly straight arms. The biceps don't get a chance to help, so the lats have to do everything — best lat-focused isolation move there is.
steps: Set a cable pulley to the highest position and attach a straight bar or rope.
Stand a step back, grip the bar shoulder-width with arms reaching overhead.
Hinge forward slightly at the hips, keeping a flat back.
Lock a soft bend in your elbows — they shouldn't change angle.
Pull the bar down in an arc to your thighs, squeezing the lats hard at the bottom.
Let the bar travel back up slowly to a full overhead stretch.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Pretend you're pushing the bar through a thick wall in front of you with your back — lats do the work, arms just transmit.
commonMistakes: Bending and straightening the elbows: turns it into a tricep press. Keep elbow angle locked.
Standing too far back: cable angle wrong, kills the lat stretch. Step in.
Using too much weight and arching the back: drop the weight and feel the lats.
tips: Great warmup for pull-day or finisher after rows — light loads with high reps work best.
Use a rope attachment to flare the hands wide at the bottom for an extra lat squeeze.

exercises.name: Assisted Pull-Up Machine
exercises.cue: Knees on pad; counterweight assists you up; greater the weight set, more the help.
exercises.description: A pull-up machine where you kneel on a pad that lifts you up — it cancels out part of your bodyweight to make pull-ups doable while you build strength. The bigger the number you set on the stack, the more weight the pad lifts off you, so heavier setting equals easier reps. Perfect for going from zero pull-ups to your first one.
steps: Set the assistance weight — start with about 50% of your bodyweight if you're brand new.
Step onto the platform and grip the pull-up bar overhead with palms facing away.
Kneel on the pad with both knees and let it lower so you're hanging with arms straight.
Brace your core and pull your shoulder blades down.
Pull yourself up by driving elbows down to your ribs until your chin clears the bar.
Lower slowly back to a full hang and repeat.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Even with the help, drive the elbows down toward your back pockets — let the back do the pulling.
commonMistakes: Setting the assistance too low and grinding ugly reps: assistance is a tool, not a sin. Use enough to do 8 clean reps.
Pushing off the pad with your knees: turns it into a leg press. Stay relaxed in the lower body.
Not lowering all the way down: cuts the stretch. Always go to a full hang.
tips: Drop the assistance by 5 kg every 1–2 weeks as the reps get easier — the goal is to graduate to unassisted pull-ups.
Use the same machine for assisted dips by flipping to the parallel handles — common feature in Indian gyms.

exercises.name: Reverse-Grip Lat Pulldown
exercises.cue: Supinated grip shoulder-width; pull bar to upper chest; greater biceps + lower-lat involvement.
exercises.description: A lat pulldown done with an underhand grip (palms facing you) instead of overhand. The reverse grip lets your elbows drive straight down past your ribs, which fires up the lower lats and pulls the biceps deeper into the lift. Many lifters feel their back better with this variation than with a standard pulldown.
steps: Attach a straight bar to the lat pulldown.
Grip the bar shoulder-width apart with palms facing you (underhand).
Sit down and lock the thigh pad firmly against your legs.
Lean back about 15 degrees and pull shoulder blades down.
Pull the bar to your upper chest by driving elbows straight down past your ribs.
Squeeze the lats at the bottom, then let the bar travel back up to a full stretch.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel your elbows trying to punch the floor — the lats pull the elbows down, the bar just comes with them.
commonMistakes: Using a too-wide grip: kills the bicep-assist and stresses the wrists. Stay shoulder-width.
Leaning back too far: turns it into a row. Keep the lean at 15°.
Stopping short of the chest: shortchanges the lats. Pull until the bar touches your upper chest.
tips: Rotate this with standard wide-grip pulldowns through the week — different grips hit different lat fibers.
Most Indian gym pulldown bars rotate freely — make sure both hands stay aligned underhand throughout the rep.

exercises.name: Barbell Overhead Press
exercises.cue: Bar starts on front delts; press straight; head through at lockout.
exercises.description: The classic standing press. You hold a barbell at your shoulders and press it straight overhead until your arms lock out. It builds shoulder size and strength, hammers the triceps, and forces your entire core to brace hard — one of the most honest tests of upper-body strength.
steps: Set the bar in a rack at upper chest height.
Grip the bar just outside shoulder-width and unrack it onto your front delts.
Step back, plant feet shoulder-width apart, and brace your core.
Tuck your chin slightly and press the bar straight up.
As the bar passes your forehead, push your head through so the bar finishes overhead, not in front.
Lock out fully, then lower the bar back to your front delts with control.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel like you're pushing the ceiling away with your shoulders while your whole body stays as tight as a steel cable.
commonMistakes: Pressing the bar in front instead of straight up: stresses the shoulder. Push your head through at the top.
Leaning back to fake leverage: turns it into an incline press and risks the low back. Keep ribs over hips.
Loose core: leaks power and bends the spine. Brace like someone's about to punch your stomach.
tips: Start lighter than you'd expect — overhead pressing is humbling. Aim for 50% of your bench press.
If a full standing press hurts your lower back, do it seated against an upright bench.

exercises.name: Dumbbell Shoulder Press
exercises.cue: Seated upright; press until arms vertical; no slamming lockout.
exercises.description: Seated or standing, you press two dumbbells overhead. Each arm works independently, which fixes left-right imbalances and lets the shoulders move through a more natural path than a barbell forces. Friendlier on the shoulders for most people than barbell overhead press.
steps: Sit on an upright bench with the back pad at about 85–90 degrees.
Pick up a dumbbell in each hand and rest them on your thighs.
Use your thighs to kick the dumbbells up to shoulder level, palms facing forward.
Brace your core and pull your shoulder blades down.
Press both dumbbells straight up until your arms are vertical.
Lower slowly back to shoulder level — stop where you feel a stretch, not pain.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Drive the dumbbells through the ceiling with your shoulders, like you're trying to grow taller.
commonMistakes: Pressing in an arc that brings the dumbbells together at the top: kills shoulder tension. Press straight up.
Letting the back arch off the pad: turns it into an incline press. Stay pinned.
Going too deep at the bottom: risks shoulder strain. Stop at shoulder level.
tips: Neutral grip (palms facing each other) is friendlier on cranky shoulders — most Indian gym dumbbells have round heads so you can rotate freely.
Pair with lateral raises for a complete shoulder day — pressing builds front delts, raises build side delts.

exercises.name: Arnold Press
exercises.cue: Start palms-in at shoulder; rotate as you press up.
exercises.description: Named after Arnold Schwarzenegger, this dumbbell press starts with palms facing you at shoulder level and rotates to palms facing forward as you press up. The rotation hits all three heads of the shoulder in one rep — front, side, and a bit of rear.
steps: Sit on an upright bench with dumbbells held in front of your shoulders, palms facing your face.
Elbows are tucked in front of the chest at the start.
Brace your core.
Begin pressing up while rotating the dumbbells outward.
By the time the dumbbells reach overhead, palms should face forward and arms vertical.
Reverse the motion on the way down, ending back at palms-in at the shoulders.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the whole shoulder cap working as the dumbbells twist — front delt at the start, side delt by the top.
commonMistakes: Rotating too early or too late: rotation should happen during the press, not before or after.
Rushing the reps: the rotation needs time to feel each phase. Slow it down.
Going too heavy: bad rotation under load tweaks the shoulder joint. Stay moderate.
tips: Start at about 70% of your regular dumbbell press weight while you learn the rotation.
Great variation when standard dumbbell press feels stale or one part of the shoulder is lagging.

exercises.name: Machine Shoulder Press
exercises.cue: Adjust seat so handles are at shoulder height; press straight up.
exercises.description: A seated machine overhead press with handles that travel in a fixed arc. The machine balances the weight for you, so you can focus completely on pushing hard with the shoulders. Great for high-rep finishers or as a starter when free-weight pressing feels intimidating.
steps: Adjust the seat so the handles are level with the tops of your shoulders.
Sit with your back against the pad and feet flat.
Grip the handles with palms facing forward (or neutral if the machine offers it).
Brace your core.
Press the handles straight up until arms are nearly straight.
Lower slowly back to shoulder level under control.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: All effort into the shoulders — the machine is doing the balance work for you, so push with intent.
commonMistakes: Seat too low or too high: shoulders end up cranked. Handles must start at shoulder level.
Locking elbows hard at the top: dumps tension. Stop just shy of lockout.
Banging the stack on the way down: lose the eccentric, lose the gains. Lower under control.
tips: Use a neutral grip (handles facing each other) if your shoulders feel beat up — it's the friendliest pressing angle.
Best place to chase failure or do drop sets on shoulder day — no risk of getting pinned.

exercises.name: Dumbbell Lateral Raise
exercises.cue: Lead with elbows; stop at shoulder height; thumb slightly down.
exercises.description: The classic side-delt builder. Standing with a dumbbell in each hand, you raise them out to the sides until they're level with your shoulders. This is the move that creates that wide, capped shoulder look — pressing alone won't do it.
steps: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, dumbbells at your sides, palms facing in.
Keep a soft, fixed bend in your elbows — don't change the angle.
Lean forward very slightly at the hips.
Raise both arms out to the sides by driving your elbows up and out.
Stop when arms are parallel with the floor — thumbs slightly lower than pinkies.
Lower slowly under control, no swing, and repeat.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Imagine pouring two jugs of water — pinkies tip up slightly, elbows lead the way out.
commonMistakes: Swinging the body to lift heavier weights: trains momentum, not the side delt. Stay still.
Raising above shoulder height: shifts work to the traps. Stop at parallel.
Straightening then re-bending the elbows: turns it into a strange front raise. Lock the bend.
tips: This is one place where going lighter beats going heavier — 5–8 kg with great form beats 12 kg with swings.
Try doing one arm at a time leaning sideways from a cable or rack — the longer range of motion really lights up the side delt.

exercises.name: Cable Lateral Raise
exercises.cue: Cable from low pulley; cross body; better stretch tension than dumbbell version.
exercises.description: A side raise done with a low cable instead of a dumbbell. The cable keeps the side delt under load even at the bottom of the rep, where a dumbbell loses tension. Often produces a better feel and pump than the dumbbell version, especially on the side delt fibers.
steps: Set a cable pulley to the lowest position with a single-handle attachment.
Stand sideways to the stack with the working arm on the far side of the body.
Reach across and grip the handle so the cable crosses behind your hip.
Stand tall with a small forward lean.
Raise your arm out to the side, leading with the elbow, until parallel with the floor.
Lower slowly across your body, feeling the side delt stretch at the bottom.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the side delt pulling the cable up like a window blind cord — slow and even on the way up, even slower on the way down.
commonMistakes: Standing too close to the stack: kills the stretch. Step out until you feel tension at the bottom.
Letting the elbow bend and straighten: turns it into a press. Lock the elbow angle.
Going too heavy and swinging: drop the weight to feel the muscle.
tips: If your gym's cable crossover has tall poles, you can do this as a 'lean-away' raise — really emphasizes the stretch position.
Pair with dumbbell laterals — cables train stretch tension, dumbbells train peak contraction.

exercises.name: Face Pull
exercises.cue: Rope to nose level; pull elbows high and wide; external rotate at end.
exercises.description: A rope pull at face height that trains the rear delts and the small muscles that hold your shoulder together. It's one of the most important exercises for keeping your shoulders healthy when you bench a lot — every gym-goer should do these.
steps: Set a cable pulley to slightly above head height with a rope attachment.
Grip each end of the rope with thumbs facing you.
Step back to load the cable and stand with feet split for balance.
Pull the rope toward your face by driving elbows high and wide.
At the end, your hands should be at your ears with palms facing forward — external rotation.
Return slowly under control to a long-arm stretch.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Try to make a goal-post shape at the end — elbows up, hands above the elbows, rear delts squeezed tight.
commonMistakes: Pulling with arms only and not the elbows: trains biceps, not rear delts. Lead with elbows high.
Cable too low: turns it into a row. Set it above head height.
Going too heavy and turning it into a row: drop the weight and feel the rear delts.
tips: Do these at the end of every push day — they balance out all the chest pressing.
Stay light — face pulls are about feel and rotator-cuff health, not heavy load.

exercises.name: Reverse Pec Deck
exercises.cue: Pull arms back in arc; squeeze rear delts, not mid-back.
exercises.description: The pec deck machine used in reverse — you face the pad and pull the handles outward instead of inward. It isolates the rear delts beautifully and removes any need for balance, so you can squeeze hard every rep.
steps: Adjust the seat so the handles line up with your shoulders.
Sit facing the pad, chest pressed against it.
Grip the handles with arms straight in front, palms facing in or down.
Pull both arms back in a wide arc until they're roughly in line with your shoulders.
Pause and squeeze the rear delts hard.
Return slowly under control to the start.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the back of your shoulders pulling your elbows behind you — the arms are just along for the ride.
commonMistakes: Pulling with the mid-back: shifts work off the rear delts. Keep shoulder blades neutral.
Pulling too far past your shoulder line: stresses the front of the shoulder. Stop at parallel.
Bending the elbows to lift more: turns it into a row. Keep them mostly straight.
tips: Use a neutral grip (palms facing each other) for a more direct rear delt hit.
Most pec deck machines in Indian gyms support both directions — just swap the seat position and adjust the handle pins.

exercises.name: Cable Reverse Fly
exercises.cue: Cross cables at chest; arc out and back; minimal trap involvement.
exercises.description: A standing rear-delt fly done at the cable crossover. You cross the cables in front and arc your arms wide to the sides. The cables keep constant tension on the rear delts through the whole rep, which is why this beats dumbbell rear flies for most people.
steps: Set both cable pulleys to chest height with single-handle attachments.
Stand in the middle and grab the opposite handle in each hand so the cables cross in front of you.
Step back to load the cables.
Lock a soft bend in your elbows.
Pull your arms out and back in a wide arc, finishing with arms behind your shoulders.
Squeeze the rear delts, then let the cables pull your arms back across in a controlled stretch.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel like you're pulling open a heavy pair of curtains with the back of your shoulders.
commonMistakes: Shrugging up during the pull: lets the traps take over. Keep shoulders down.
Bending the elbows to row: turns it into a row. Lock the elbow angle.
Standing too close to the stacks: kills the stretch. Step back.
tips: Great alternative when the reverse pec deck is taken — same muscle, similar feel.
Use light weight and focus on a clean arc — rear delts respond to feel, not load.

exercises.name: Dumbbell Front Raise
exercises.cue: Front delts already worked by pressing; use sparingly as a finisher.
exercises.description: Standing with dumbbells at your thighs, you raise them in front of you to shoulder height. Front delts already get hammered by every pressing movement (bench, overhead, push-up), so this is best treated as a small finisher rather than a main shoulder exercise.
steps: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, dumbbell in each hand, arms at sides.
Palms can face in or down — pick whichever feels better on your shoulder.
Keep a slight bend in the elbow and lock it in.
Raise both arms forward and up until they're roughly parallel with the floor.
Pause briefly at the top.
Lower slowly back to your thighs and repeat.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel just the very front of the shoulder lifting the weights — like raising a flag.
commonMistakes: Swinging the body to lift heavier: kills isolation. Stay still.
Going above shoulder height: shifts work to the traps. Stop at parallel.
Doing too much volume on front raises while still pressing heavy: overworks an already-trained muscle.
tips: If you press 3+ times a week, you probably don't need this. Skip it for more lateral raises or rear-delt work.
Alternate arms instead of lifting both at once — easier on the lower back.

exercises.name: Barbell Curl
exercises.cue: Elbows pinned to sides; control the lower more than the lift.
exercises.description: The classic biceps builder. You hold a barbell with palms facing up and curl it from your thighs to your chest. Because both hands are locked to the bar, you can load it heavier than any other curl variation — great for building biceps mass.
steps: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, grip the barbell shoulder-width with palms facing up.
Let the bar hang at your thighs with arms straight.
Pin your elbows to your sides — they don't move forward or back during the rep.
Curl the bar up to chest level by bending only at the elbows.
Squeeze the biceps hard at the top.
Lower slowly back to a long-arm stretch — control the eccentric for 2 seconds.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Pretend your elbows are nails in the wall — only your forearms swing, biceps do all the lifting.
commonMistakes: Swinging the body to lift the weight: turns it into a back exercise. Stay still or strap to a wall.
Elbows drifting forward: shifts work to the front delt. Pin them at your sides.
Half reps: shortchanges the stretch. Go all the way down and all the way up.
tips: If a straight bar bothers your wrists, swap to an EZ-bar — most Indian gyms have one near the curl rack.
On the last set, drop the weight by 30% and do an extra 10 reps as a drop set for a great pump finisher.

exercises.name: Dumbbell Curl
exercises.cue: Supinate as you curl; full ROM at the bottom; alternating or together.
exercises.description: Curls with a dumbbell in each hand. Because your hands can rotate, you twist the palms up as you curl — that rotation (supination) is what fully activates the biceps. You can curl both at once or alternate arms.
steps: Stand with a dumbbell in each hand, arms at sides, palms facing in.
Pin elbows to your sides.
Curl the dumbbells up while rotating the wrists so palms end up facing the shoulders at the top.
Squeeze the biceps hard at the peak.
Lower slowly while rotating back to palms-in at the bottom.
Repeat with both arms or alternate.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the biceps shorten and ball up as the palms twist toward you — the twist is what makes them flex hardest.
commonMistakes: Not rotating the wrists: skips half the biceps activation. Twist as you curl.
Elbows swinging forward at the top: takes load off the biceps. Pin them.
Body swing: trains momentum. Strict reps win.
tips: Alternating arms lets you focus on one side at a time — fixes left-right imbalances.
Pause for one count at the top with palms fully twisted up — that's the peak biceps position.

exercises.name: Hammer Curl
exercises.cue: Neutral grip; curl across body to opposite shoulder for peak contraction.
exercises.description: A dumbbell curl done with palms facing each other the whole way — like you're swinging a hammer. The neutral grip targets a different part of the biceps (the brachialis) and the brachioradialis on the forearm. Adds thickness to the arms that regular curls can miss.
steps: Stand with a dumbbell in each hand, arms at sides, palms facing your thighs.
Pin elbows to your sides — they don't move.
Curl the dumbbells up keeping palms facing each other.
For peak contraction, curl across your body toward the opposite shoulder.
Squeeze at the top for a beat.
Lower slowly back to your sides and repeat.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the side of the upper arm and the top of the forearm working together to crank the dumbbell up.
commonMistakes: Rotating the wrist: turns it back into a regular curl. Keep palms facing each other.
Elbows flaring out: shifts load. Pin them at the sides.
Too heavy and swinging: drop the weight and feel the brachialis.
tips: Cross-body version (curling toward the opposite shoulder) gives a stronger peak squeeze than straight up.
Pair with a regular dumbbell curl in the same workout — hammer for thickness, supinated curl for peak height.

exercises.name: Preacher Curl
exercises.cue: Pad in armpit; don't fully extend at the bottom, protect the elbow.
exercises.description: A curl done with the upper arms locked on the angled pad of a preacher bench. The pad takes all body swing out of the lift, so the biceps work in pure isolation. The bottom of the rep is especially hard, which makes preacher curls great for building biceps strength in the stretched position.
steps: Adjust the preacher bench so the pad fits snugly against your armpits.
Sit with chest against the pad and grip an EZ-bar or barbell with palms up.
Have someone hand you the bar or pick it up with the help of a foot prop.
Lower the bar slowly until your arms are almost straight — stop short of full lockout to protect the elbow.
Curl the bar up by bending at the elbow only.
Squeeze the biceps at the top, then lower with control.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the lower part of the biceps doing all the work at the bottom of the rep — it's the hardest part.
commonMistakes: Fully locking the elbows at the bottom: stresses the joint. Stop just shy.
Lifting the chest off the pad to swing the bar up: defeats the isolation. Stay glued.
Going too heavy: this is a feel exercise. Drop the weight.
tips: Use an EZ-bar instead of a straight bar — much friendlier on the wrists.
Indian gyms often have preacher benches at fixed angles — if yours feels too steep, do dumbbell preacher curls one arm at a time and lean slightly.

exercises.name: Incline Dumbbell Curl
exercises.cue: Bench at ~60°; let arms hang behind torso for stretched-position bias.
exercises.description: A dumbbell curl done lying back on an incline bench. The bench angle pulls your arms behind your torso, putting the biceps in a stretched position before you even start. That stretched-position curling is one of the best stimuli for biceps growth.
steps: Set an adjustable bench to about 60 degrees.
Sit back with a dumbbell in each hand, arms hanging straight down at your sides.
Let the dumbbells stretch the biceps fully — arms slightly behind your torso.
Curl both dumbbells up while rotating palms to face you.
Pin the elbows so they don't drift forward.
Lower slowly back to a full stretch and repeat.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel a deep stretch in the biceps at the bottom of every rep — like the muscle is being pulled long.
commonMistakes: Lifting elbows forward to shorten the lift: kills the stretch. Keep elbows pinned.
Going too heavy: the stretched position is harder. Drop weight by 30% from your standing curl.
Bouncing out of the bottom: tears at the biceps tendon. Pause briefly and curl smoothly.
tips: Hold the bottom stretch for a 1-second count on the last set for an extra growth boost.
Best done after compound back work — biceps are pre-fatigued and respond extra well to the stretch.

exercises.name: Cable Curl
exercises.cue: Constant tension throughout; pause and squeeze at the peak.
exercises.description: A curl at the cable station, usually with a straight bar attached to a low pulley. Unlike dumbbells and barbells where the load drops off at the top of the curl, the cable keeps tension on the biceps the whole way — great for a deep pump.
steps: Set a cable pulley to the lowest setting and attach a straight or EZ-bar.
Stand a step back from the stack with feet shoulder-width.
Grip the bar palms up, shoulder-width.
Pin elbows to your sides.
Curl the bar up to chest level, squeezing the biceps hard.
Lower slowly while keeping tension on the cable — don't let it yank your arms forward.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the constant tug on the biceps — they're under load even at the top, unlike free weights.
commonMistakes: Standing too close to the stack: kills the tension at the top. Step back.
Body leaning forward as you curl: turns it into a row. Stay upright.
Letting the cable drag the arms down too fast: lose the eccentric. Control the lower.
tips: Switch the attachment — rope for hammer-style cable curls, single-handle for one-arm work.
Great finisher after barbell or dumbbell curls — the constant tension creates serious pump.

exercises.name: Concentration Curl
exercises.cue: Elbow against inner thigh; isolate; squeeze hard at top.
exercises.description: A seated single-arm dumbbell curl where you brace your elbow against the inside of your thigh. The leg locks the elbow in place so the biceps does all the work. Classic finisher move for chasing peak contraction.
steps: Sit on a bench with feet wide apart, dumbbell in one hand.
Lean forward slightly and brace the back of your working arm against the inside of the same-side thigh.
Let the dumbbell hang straight down, arm fully extended.
Curl the dumbbell up to your shoulder, rotating the palm to face you at the top.
Squeeze hard at the peak for a 1-second count.
Lower slowly back to a full stretch.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: All you should feel is the biceps balling up — the leg holds the elbow, the biceps does the curling.
commonMistakes: Lifting the elbow off the thigh: defeats the brace. Keep it locked.
Going too heavy and using the shoulder: drop the weight.
Rushing reps: this is a feel exercise. Slow it down.
tips: Best as a finisher — go light, chase the squeeze, do 3 sets of 12–15.
Hold the peak contraction for 2 seconds on the last few reps.

exercises.name: Close-Grip Bench Press
exercises.cue: Hands shoulder-width; tuck elbows; bar to lower sternum.
exercises.description: A bench press with hands placed shoulder-width apart instead of wider. The narrower grip shifts most of the work onto the triceps while still letting you load heavy weight. Builds bigger arms and a stronger regular bench press in one move.
steps: Lie on a flat bench and grip the bar shoulder-width apart (index fingers on the smooth ring or just inside it).
Plant feet, squeeze shoulder blades down and together.
Unrack the bar and hold it over your shoulders.
Lower the bar slowly to your lower sternum, keeping elbows tucked tight to your body.
Press back up by extending the elbows hard.
Lock out fully — triceps drive the lockout.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the back of your arms doing the pressing — like pushing the bar up with your triceps, not your chest.
commonMistakes: Grip too narrow: stresses the wrists. Keep hands at shoulder-width or just slightly inside.
Flaring elbows: turns it back into a chest press. Tuck them tight.
Lowering too high (chest): hits the chest more than the triceps. Bring bar to lower sternum.
tips: Use this on a triceps day or as your second pressing move on chest day.
Start at about 70% of your regular bench press — the narrow grip is humbling.

exercises.name: Cable Tricep Pushdown
exercises.cue: Elbows pinned at ribs; full lockout; rope or straight bar both work.
exercises.description: Standing at a cable station with the pulley high, you push a bar or rope down by extending your elbows. The cable keeps tension on the triceps through the whole range, which makes this one of the most reliable triceps isolation exercises.
steps: Set a cable pulley to the top and attach a straight bar, V-bar, or rope.
Stand a step back from the stack with feet split for balance.
Grip the attachment with palms down (for bars) or facing each other (for rope).
Pin elbows tight against your ribs.
Push the attachment straight down by extending the elbows.
Lock out fully and squeeze the triceps for a beat, then return slowly.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the back of the upper arm punching downward — elbows stay glued, only the forearms move.
commonMistakes: Elbows drifting forward: shifts load to the chest. Keep them at your ribs.
Leaning over to push more weight: turns it into a press. Stay upright.
Half reps: skip the squeeze. Lock out fully every rep.
tips: Rotate attachments — rope for triceps spread at the bottom, straight bar for heavier load.
Last set: drop the weight by 30% and rep out for a brutal pump finisher.

exercises.name: Overhead Tricep Extension (Cable)
exercises.cue: Arms by ears at top; deep stretch — long head responds best to overhead.
exercises.description: A triceps extension done with the cable behind you, arms going overhead. The overhead position puts the long head of the triceps (the biggest of the three) in a deep stretch, which is the key stimulus for that part of the muscle. Often gives better arm growth than pushdowns alone.
steps: Set a cable pulley to the lowest setting and attach a rope.
Face away from the stack, grab the rope behind your head, and step forward.
Stagger your feet and lean slightly forward.
Start with arms bent, hands behind your head, elbows pointing up by your ears.
Extend your arms forward and up until they're nearly straight overhead.
Lower slowly back to the deep stretch position and repeat.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel a long stretch under the back of your upper arms at the bottom — that's the long head loading up.
commonMistakes: Elbows flaring out wide: shortens the long head. Keep elbows by your ears.
Standing too close to the stack: kills the stretch. Step out further.
Going too heavy and arching the back: drop the weight.
tips: Best paired with cable pushdowns — pushdowns hit the long head short, overhead extensions hit it long.
Hold the bottom stretch for a 1-second count on the last set for extra growth signal.

exercises.name: Skull Crusher (EZ-Bar)
exercises.cue: EZ-bar; lower to forehead or just behind head; keep elbows in.
exercises.description: A lying triceps extension done with an EZ-bar. You hold the bar over your chest and lower it toward your forehead by bending only at the elbows. Despite the scary name, it's one of the best triceps mass builders when done with control.
steps: Lie on a flat bench with an EZ-bar in your hands, arms straight over your chest.
Tilt your arms back slightly so they angle toward your head — about 15 degrees.
Pin your elbows in place; they shouldn't move forward or back during the rep.
Bend at the elbows and lower the bar slowly to your forehead or just past it.
Press the bar back up by extending the elbows, keeping the arm angle constant.
Stop just shy of lockout to keep tension on the triceps.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Picture the back of your arms hinging open and closed like a pair of scissors — elbows stay fixed in space.
commonMistakes: Elbows flaring wide: makes the lift sloppy and strains the joint. Pin them.
Holding arms perfectly vertical: makes the lockout too easy. Tilt them back 15°.
Going too heavy and dropping the bar on your face: this is a feel exercise. Stay moderate.
tips: Use an EZ-bar, not a straight bar — your wrists will thank you.
Lower toward the spot just behind the top of your head, not your forehead — more stretch on the long head of the triceps.

exercises.name: Dip (Tricep Bias)
exercises.cue: Stay vertical to bias triceps over chest; controlled descent.
exercises.description: A bodyweight dip done with the torso held upright instead of leaning forward. The upright posture pulls the work onto the triceps and front shoulders rather than the chest. Add load with a dip belt as you get stronger for a serious arm builder.
steps: Grip the parallel bars and press up to a straight-arm support position.
Cross ankles behind you and brace your core.
Keep the torso vertical — chest up, ribs over hips.
Lower yourself by bending at the elbows, keeping them tucked tight to your sides.
Stop when your upper arms are roughly parallel with the floor.
Press straight back up by extending the elbows, locking out at the top.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the back of your upper arms doing all the work — like a tricep pushdown, but it's your body that moves.
commonMistakes: Leaning forward: shifts work to the chest. Stay vertical.
Elbows flaring out wide: takes load off triceps. Tuck them.
Dropping too deep: cranks the shoulder. Stop at parallel.
tips: If your gym's dip station rocks, use the assisted machine for solo dips with a steady frame.
Add a dip belt once you can do 12 strict bodyweight reps.

exercises.name: JM Press
exercises.cue: Hybrid skull-crusher and close-grip; tuck elbows, lower to throat.
exercises.description: A hybrid between a skull crusher and a close-grip bench, named after powerlifter J.M. Blakley. You lower the bar to your throat with the bar staying close to your body and elbows tucked. Brutal on the triceps and lets you handle much heavier loads than skull crushers.
steps: Lie on a flat bench and grip the bar shoulder-width apart.
Unrack the bar and hold it over your shoulders.
Lower the bar slowly toward your throat by bending the elbows, keeping them tucked.
The bar should stay closer to your face than in a regular bench press.
When the bar is near your throat with elbows fully bent, reverse and press back up.
Lock out and reset for the next rep.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the triceps shouldering the entire weight as the bar tracks close to your face.
commonMistakes: Letting elbows flare wide: defeats the lift. Tuck them tight.
Letting the bar drift forward like a regular bench: keep it traveling toward the throat.
Going too heavy too soon: this lift takes practice. Start light.
tips: Strange-looking lift — use a spotter the first few times you try it.
Best for intermediate to advanced lifters chasing extra triceps stimulus on a press day.

exercises.name: Tricep Kickback
exercises.cue: Elbow high and pinned; extend, squeeze, control return.
exercises.description: A triceps isolation done leaning over, where you pin your upper arm parallel with your torso and extend your forearm back behind you. Easy on the joints and gives a strong peak contraction at the back of the rep.
steps: Stand with a dumbbell in one hand and hinge your torso to nearly parallel with the floor.
Support yourself with the free hand on a bench.
Pin the working elbow at your side with the upper arm parallel to the floor.
Start with the elbow bent at 90 degrees, forearm hanging straight down.
Extend the elbow back, straightening the arm fully behind you.
Squeeze the triceps at the top, then lower slowly to the start.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the triceps cramp at the top as you push the dumbbell straight back behind you.
commonMistakes: Elbow drops below parallel: kills the contraction. Pin the upper arm.
Swinging the dumbbell with momentum: trains nothing. Stay strict.
Going too heavy: ruins the squeeze. Stay light.
tips: Best as a finisher — go light, do 12–15 reps, chase the squeeze.
Try the cable version (low pulley, attached to a single handle) for constant tension if dumbbells lose feel at the top.

exercises.name: Bench Dip
exercises.cue: Hands on bench behind; keep feet close to limit shoulder strain.
exercises.description: A simple triceps move where you sit on the edge of a bench, place your hands beside your hips, and dip down by bending the elbows. Easy to set up anywhere — but the position is hard on the shoulders, so use it as a finisher rather than a main triceps move.
steps: Sit on the edge of a bench with hands gripping the edge beside your hips.
Slide your butt off the bench and support yourself with arms straight.
Keep feet close to the bench for less shoulder strain (or extended out for more difficulty).
Lower yourself by bending the elbows until upper arms are parallel with the floor.
Press back up by extending the elbows.
Stop just shy of lockout to keep tension on the triceps.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the back of your upper arms doing all the lifting — like pushing the bench down under you.
commonMistakes: Dropping too deep: brutal on the shoulders. Stop at parallel.
Elbows flaring wide: shifts load. Keep them pointing back.
Hunching the shoulders: stay tall, chest up.
tips: If shoulders hurt, switch to parallel-bar dips or cable pushdowns instead.
Add load by placing a plate on your thighs once bodyweight feels easy.

exercises.name: Barbell Back Squat
exercises.cue: Bar on traps; brace; hips and knees move together; depth at parallel or below.
exercises.description: The king of lower-body lifts. You rest a loaded barbell across your upper back, squat down until your thighs hit at least parallel with the floor, and stand back up. Builds quads, glutes, and a fortress-strong core all at once. Worth the time it takes to learn well.
steps: Set the bar in a rack at upper chest height.
Duck under the bar and rest it across your upper traps, just below your neck.
Grip the bar wider than shoulder-width, elbows pointing down.
Unrack and step back with feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly turned out.
Take a big breath, brace the core, and squat down by pushing hips back and knees out.
Descend until thighs are at least parallel with the floor.
Drive up through the whole foot, exhaling at the top, and stand fully upright.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel like you're squeezing the floor with your feet and pushing the earth down on every rep.
commonMistakes: Knees caving in: weakens the lift and risks injury. Push knees out in line with toes.
Heels lifting off the floor: tight ankles. Use lifting shoes or wedge plates under heels temporarily.
Rounding the lower back at the bottom: drop the weight and improve depth gradually.
tips: Most Indian gym racks are a bit narrow — check that the safety pins are set at your bottom squat depth before loading heavy.
Start with goblet squats (dumbbell at chest) for a month before adding the barbell if you're new to squatting.

exercises.name: Front Squat
exercises.cue: Bar on front delts; elbows high; upright torso biases quads.
exercises.description: A squat with the bar resting on the front of the shoulders instead of the back. The position forces an upright torso, which throws more work onto the quads and less on the lower back. Harder to balance than a back squat — but lighter loads with more quad activation.
steps: Set the bar in a rack at upper chest height.
Place the bar across the front of your shoulders, resting on the front delts.
Grip the bar with fingertips wider than shoulders, elbows up high and pointing forward.
Unrack and step back with feet shoulder-width apart.
Take a breath, brace hard, and squat down keeping the torso vertical.
Descend until thighs are at or below parallel.
Drive up through your feet, keeping the elbows high all the way.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel like a string is pulling your elbows up to the ceiling — that's what keeps the bar safe and the quads loaded.
commonMistakes: Elbows drop: bar starts rolling forward. Cue elbows up every rep.
Leaning forward at the bottom: bar will fall off. Stay vertical.
Wrists hurt under the bar: stretch wrist mobility, use a crossed-arm grip if needed.
tips: Start at about 70% of your back squat weight.
Use a crossed-arm grip (arms crossed in front of the bar) if your wrist mobility is limited.

exercises.name: Leg Press
exercises.cue: Feet shoulder-width on platform; full ROM; never hard-lock the knees.
exercises.description: A machine version of the squat where you sit back and push a weighted platform with your legs. Removes balance demands and lower-back loading, so you can train the quads hard with very heavy weights. Most-loved leg machine in any gym for good reason.
steps: Sit on the leg press with your back firmly against the pad.
Place feet shoulder-width apart in the middle of the platform.
Release the safety latches and grip the side handles.
Lower the platform slowly toward your chest by bending the knees.
Stop when your knees reach about 90 degrees or just past — keep the lower back flat against the pad.
Press the platform back up by pushing through your whole foot.
Stop just shy of locked knees, then repeat.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Push the platform away with the front of your thighs — quads do all the work.
commonMistakes: Locking knees hard at the top: stresses the joint. Stop just shy.
Lower back curling off the pad at the bottom: limits how deep you should go.
Feet too low on the platform: blasts the quads but stresses the knees if you go too low.
tips: Foot position changes the bias — higher on platform for more hamstring/glute, lower for more quad.
Indian gym leg presses are usually 45-degree sleds — heavier than horizontal presses, so load conservatively the first time.

exercises.name: Hack Squat (Machine)
exercises.cue: Feet lower on platform for quad bias; sit deep, drive through whole foot.
exercises.description: A machine squat where you stand on a platform with your back against an angled pad. The fixed path lets you push hard on the quads without worrying about balance. Especially good for hitting deep squat positions safely.
steps: Step onto the platform with your back firmly against the pad.
Position shoulders under the shoulder pads.
Place feet shoulder-width apart, slightly lower on the platform for quad bias.
Release the safety handles.
Lower yourself slowly by bending the knees, sitting deep into the squat.
Drive back up by pushing through the whole foot.
Stop short of full knee lockout, then repeat.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the quads loading hard at the bottom, then exploding the platform up like a piston.
commonMistakes: Heels lifting at the bottom: feet too low. Adjust foot placement up slightly.
Locking knees hard: dangerous on a loaded machine. Stop short.
Half reps: skip the depth, skip the growth. Go deep.
tips: Better than back squats for many people because there's no lower-back loading.
Try paused reps — sit at the bottom for 2 seconds, then drive up — for a brutal quad stimulus.

exercises.name: Bulgarian Split Squat
exercises.cue: Rear foot elevated; drop straight down; front leg does the work.
exercises.description: A single-leg squat with the rear foot resting on a bench behind you. Each leg works on its own, which fixes left-right strength imbalances and gives a brutal stimulus to the quads and glutes. One of the most effective single-leg exercises ever.
steps: Stand about two feet in front of a bench with a dumbbell in each hand.
Place the top of your back foot on the bench behind you.
Plant the front foot far enough out that your front knee can bend without going past your toes.
Drop straight down by bending the front knee.
Stop when your front thigh is parallel with the floor.
Drive back up through the front heel, keeping the torso upright.
Finish all reps on one leg before switching sides.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the front leg doing 90% of the work — the back leg is just a kickstand for balance.
commonMistakes: Front foot too close to the bench: forces the knee past the toes. Step further out.
Pushing off the rear foot: defeats the unilateral training. Front leg drives.
Losing torso position: stay upright, ribs over hips.
tips: Start with bodyweight only until you can do 12 strict reps per leg.
