Hold the dumbbells at your sides for easier balance, or in a goblet position for more quad bias.

exercises.name: Walking Lunge
exercises.cue: Long step; back knee taps the floor; push off the front heel.
exercises.description: Walking forward by alternating long lunge steps with a dumbbell in each hand. Each rep is a single-leg squat with momentum carrying you into the next step. Trains the legs, balance, and athleticism all at once.
steps: Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand, arms at your sides.
Step forward a long stride with one leg.
Drop straight down, lowering your back knee until it taps the floor.
Drive up through your front heel and bring the back leg forward into the next step.
Continue stepping forward, alternating legs.
Aim for 8–12 steps per leg per set.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the front leg doing the lift on each step — push the ground down to stand up.
commonMistakes: Short stride: knee goes past the toes. Take a longer step.
Back knee slamming the floor: tap lightly, don't crash.
Torso leaning forward: stay upright.
tips: Need a long stretch of clear floor — many Indian gyms have narrow walkways, so use the parking area or do reverse lunges instead.
Start with light dumbbells while you learn the stride.

exercises.name: Leg Extension
exercises.cue: Seat aligned with knee axis; pause and squeeze at the top.
exercises.description: Seated at a machine, you straighten your legs by lifting a padded lever with your shins. The machine isolates the quads completely — no balance, no other muscles involved. Perfect for finishing off the quads after squats or leg press.
steps: Adjust the seat so your knees line up with the machine's pivot point.
Set the ankle pad to rest just above your ankles, not on your toes.
Sit tall, grip the side handles, and brace your core.
Extend your knees, lifting the pad until your legs are nearly straight.
Pause and squeeze the quads hard for a 1-second count at the top.
Lower slowly back to the start, stopping before the weight stack touches down.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the quads balling up tight as you lock the knees — like making a fist with your thighs.
commonMistakes: Slamming the weight up: trains momentum. Lift smoothly.
Letting the weight crash on the way down: kills the eccentric. Control the lower.
Locking knees hard at the top: hyperextension risk. Stop just shy.
tips: Pause at the top for 2 seconds on the last set for a serious quad burn.
Use this as a finisher after compound leg work, not as a main lift.

exercises.name: Step-Up
exercises.cue: Knee-height bench; drive through whole foot; no rebound off rear leg.
exercises.description: A single-leg exercise where you step up onto a bench with a dumbbell in each hand. Simple, effective, and great for fixing left-right strength imbalances. Easy to learn and friendly on the joints.
steps: Stand in front of a bench that's roughly knee-height with dumbbells at your sides.
Plant one foot fully on the bench.
Drive up through the planted foot to stand up on top of the bench.
Do not push off the trailing foot — the working leg does all the work.
Step back down with the trailing leg first.
Finish all reps on one side before switching.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel only the leg on the bench doing the work — push the bench down into the floor with your foot.
commonMistakes: Bench too high: turns into a balance challenge. Use knee-height or lower.
Pushing off the back foot: defeats the single-leg training. Keep it relaxed.
Rushing down: control the descent for muscle stimulus.
tips: Slow the lowering phase to 3 seconds for extra quad and glute work.
Use a small platform if a flat bench feels unstable in your gym.

exercises.name: Sissy Squat
exercises.cue: Knees travel forward; lean back as you sink; quad isolator, hard on knees.
exercises.description: An old-school quad isolation move where you balance on your toes and lean back as you bend your knees deeply. The knees travel forward way past the toes, which puts the quads under huge stretch. Brutal on the quads but stressful on the knees — use carefully.
steps: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a support (rack, wall) with one hand.
Rise onto the balls of your feet.
Bend the knees and let them travel forward as you lean your torso back.
Keep a straight line from knees to shoulders.
Sink as low as you can hold control, feeling the deep quad stretch.
Drive back up through the balls of your feet to the start.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the front of the thighs stretching long and tight at the bottom — pure quad isolation.
commonMistakes: Knees hurt: stop. This lift isn't for everyone. Use leg extensions instead.
Bending at the hips: kills the quad stretch. Keep knees-to-shoulders straight.
Going too low too fast: build up gradually.
tips: If your gym has a dedicated sissy squat bench (calf pads to brace), use it — much safer.
Skip this if you have any knee history. Plenty of other quad moves available.

exercises.name: Smith Machine Squat
exercises.cue: Fixed bar path; place feet slightly forward to reduce knee shear.
exercises.description: A back squat done on a Smith machine, where the bar travels along fixed rails. You lose the balance demand of a free barbell, but you gain safety and consistency. Common in Indian gyms where free racks are limited — and useful when training alone since you can rack the bar at any height by twisting your wrists.
steps: Position yourself under the Smith bar with the bar resting across your upper traps.
Twist your wrists forward to unrack the bar.
Step both feet slightly forward of the bar — about 15 cm in front — to reduce knee stress.
Brace your core and squat down by sitting back and bending the knees.
Descend until thighs are parallel with the floor or just below.
Drive up through your whole foot, keeping back against the bar's path.
Twist wrists back at the top to re-rack.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the front of your thighs powering the bar up — since the bar can't drift, all effort goes into pushing the floor away.
commonMistakes: Feet directly under the bar: bar path pushes knees over toes. Step feet forward.
Not knowing the rack mechanism: practice the twist-to-rack motion before loading.
Half reps because it 'feels safer': use the safety to go full depth, not less.
tips: The Smith machine in most Indian gyms tilts slightly forward — align your spine to the bar path, not the rack uprights.
Great for high-rep drop sets where free-weight squats would be unsafe.

exercises.name: Romanian Deadlift
exercises.cue: Soft knees; push hips back; bar drags down thighs; stop at upper shins.
exercises.description: A hip-hinge exercise where you hold a barbell and bend forward by pushing your hips back, lowering the bar down your thighs to about shin level. The hamstrings get a deep stretch under load, which is what makes RDLs one of the best hamstring builders.
steps: Stand with feet hip-width apart, bar in hands, palms down at thigh level.
Keep a soft bend in the knees — they don't bend more during the rep.
Push your hips back as far as you can while keeping a flat back.
Let the bar slide down your thighs, staying close to your legs.
Stop when you feel a strong hamstring stretch, usually around your upper shins.
Drive hips forward to stand back up, squeezing glutes at the top.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the hamstrings stretching like rubber bands as your hips push back — they pull you back upright.
commonMistakes: Bending the knees too much: turns it into a squat. Lock the knee bend.
Bar drifting forward: doubles the load on the back. Keep it brushing the legs.
Rounding the back at the bottom: stop earlier, raise the start position with blocks.
tips: Don't chase floor depth — RDLs stop when the hamstrings stretch maxes out, usually mid-shin.
Use straps once load gets heavy — your grip will fail before your hamstrings.

exercises.name: Lying Leg Curl
exercises.cue: Pad above heels; curl, squeeze, control eccentric.
exercises.description: A face-down machine where you bend your knees to curl a padded lever toward your butt. Isolates the hamstrings completely, with no balance or stability demands. Best paired with RDLs — RDLs hit the hamstrings stretched, leg curls hit them shortened.
steps: Lie face down on the machine with the ankle pad set just above your heels.
Adjust the seat so your knees align with the machine's pivot.
Grip the handles and brace your core.
Curl your heels toward your butt by bending the knees.
Squeeze the hamstrings hard at the top.
Lower slowly back to nearly straight legs, stopping before the stack touches down.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the back of your thighs squeezing tight as your heels come up — like making a fist with your hamstrings.
commonMistakes: Lifting hips off the pad to swing the lever up: defeats the isolation. Stay flat.
Going too heavy and not getting full ROM: drop the weight, get the squeeze.
Rushing the eccentric: let the weight drop. Hamstrings grow from the lower.
tips: Pause at the top for 1 second on the last set for extra growth signal.
If your gym only has seated leg curls, both versions work — they emphasize different parts of the hamstring.

exercises.name: Seated Leg Curl
exercises.cue: Hamstring stretch is greater seated; full ROM beats heavy partials.
exercises.description: A seated machine where you curl your legs down from a straight position to bent. Because your hips are flexed (you're seated), the hamstrings start in a stretched position before they curl — and stretched-position training is one of the strongest growth stimuli.
steps: Sit on the machine and adjust the seat so your knees line up with the pivot.
Set the ankle pad to just above your heels.
Lock your thighs under the thigh pad firmly.
Grip the handles and brace your core.
Curl your legs down by bending the knees against the pad.
Squeeze the hamstrings, then return slowly to nearly straight legs.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the hamstrings stretching at the top and balling up tight at the bottom of the curl.
commonMistakes: Hips lifting off the seat: defeats the stretch position. Lock yourself in.
Half reps: skip the stretch. Go full ROM.
Slamming the weight on the negative: control the lower.
tips: Many lifters get a better hamstring feel from seated curls than lying curls — try both and use the one you connect with.
Pair with RDLs for a complete hamstring program — RDLs build the muscle big, curls fill out the bottom.

exercises.name: Nordic Curl
exercises.cue: Anchor ankles; lower body slowly; eccentric powerhouse for the hamstrings.
exercises.description: A brutal bodyweight hamstring exercise. With your ankles anchored, you lower your body forward toward the floor by extending the knees, then pull yourself back up using only the hamstrings. The lowering phase is one of the strongest growth stimuli the hamstrings can get.
steps: Anchor your ankles under a bar, pads, or a partner's hands.
Start in a tall kneeling position with hips fully extended.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes.
Lower your body forward slowly by extending the knees — keep hips and back straight.
Resist the descent as long as you can, then catch yourself with your hands.
Push back to the start with arms, or use the hamstrings to pull up if you're strong enough.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the back of your thighs working overtime to fight gravity on the way down.
commonMistakes: Hinging at the hips: cheats the lift. Keep hips locked open.
Going too fast on the lower: skips the growth phase. Take 5+ seconds down.
No hand catch: face plant. Always be ready to catch.
tips: Most people can't pull themselves back up at first — use hands to assist the way up for several weeks.
Two clean sets of 5 reps is plenty — the eccentric is extremely taxing.

exercises.name: Glute-Ham Raise
exercises.cue: Hip hinge into knee flexion; trains both hamstring functions.
exercises.description: A specialized exercise done on a glute-ham raise bench (GHR). You start kneeling with feet anchored, hinge down at the hips, then curl your body back up using the hamstrings. Trains both functions of the hamstring (hip extension and knee flexion) in one move.
steps: Set up on a GHR bench with feet anchored against the foot plate.
Start in a tall kneeling position with thighs vertical on the pad.
Brace your core and lower yourself slowly by hinging at the hips.
Once your back is nearly horizontal, extend the knees to lower further until your body is straight.
Reverse by curling the knees first, then drive the hips back up.
Finish at the tall kneeling start position.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel both the top and bottom of the hamstring working — top during the hip hinge, bottom during the knee curl.
commonMistakes: Skipping the hinge phase: cuts the hamstring stimulus in half. Hinge first, then curl.
Bouncing at the bottom: risky for the hamstrings. Move smoothly.
Going too fast: trains nothing. Take 3 seconds down, 2 seconds up.
tips: Few Indian gyms have a GHR bench — if yours doesn't, use Nordic curls instead.
Start with the easier hinge-only version (no knee extension) until you build strength.

exercises.name: Good Morning
exercises.cue: Bar on traps; hinge with neutral spine; light loads, big stretch.
exercises.description: A hip-hinge done with a barbell across the upper back. You bow forward like you're greeting someone, then stand back up. Like an RDL but with the bar high — trains the hamstrings, glutes, and lower back together. Use lighter loads than you'd think.
steps: Set the bar in a rack and load it light to start.
Step under the bar and rest it across your upper traps like a back squat.
Step back, feet hip-width apart.
Keep a soft bend in the knees, brace the core.
Push hips back and bow forward, keeping the back flat.
Stop when your torso is roughly parallel with the floor or where hamstrings tap out.
Drive hips forward to stand back up, squeezing the glutes at the top.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the back of the thighs stretching long as the chest moves toward the floor.
commonMistakes: Rounding the back: dangerous with a bar on traps. Drop weight and stay flat.
Bending the knees to compensate: turns it into a squat. Lock the knee bend.
Going too heavy: this lift demands light loads. Start with 30 kg total.
tips: Use 30–40% of your back squat weight maximum.
Skip if your lower back is tight — RDLs are easier on the back.

exercises.name: Single-Leg Romanian Deadlift
exercises.cue: One leg back; hinge with flat back; balance is the limiter, not load.
exercises.description: An RDL done on one leg, with the other leg lifted behind you. The single-leg setup hammers the hamstring and glute of the standing leg while training balance and core stability. The limiting factor is balance, not strength.
steps: Hold a dumbbell in one or both hands, stand on one leg with a soft knee bend.
Lift the other leg slightly off the floor behind you.
Hinge at the hips, pushing the back leg straight out behind you.
Lower the dumbbells toward the floor while keeping a flat back.
Body forms a straight line from head to lifted heel.
Drive the hips forward to return to standing, controlling the working leg.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the standing-leg hamstring stretching long, then pulling you back upright like a hinge.
commonMistakes: Rotating the hips: misaligns the body. Keep both hip bones pointing at the floor.
Letting the back round: focus on a long, flat back like an RDL.
Putting the lifted foot down for balance: defeats the unilateral training. Stay on one leg.
tips: Use light dumbbells — balance is the limiter, not load.
Stare at a fixed point on the floor 3 meters ahead to help balance.

exercises.name: Stiff-Leg Deadlift
exercises.cue: Minimal knee bend; deeper than RDL; bar can lightly touch the floor.
exercises.description: A deadlift done with the legs nearly straight throughout. Similar to an RDL, but you go all the way down until the bar touches the floor instead of stopping at shin level. Maximum hamstring stretch with a deeper range of motion.
steps: Stand with feet hip-width, bar over mid-foot, grip just outside the legs.
Keep a very slight knee bend — almost straight, but not locked.
Hinge at the hips, lowering the bar all the way to the floor.
Keep the back flat and the bar close to your legs the whole way.
Stop when the bar lightly touches the floor or you've reached max hamstring stretch.
Drive the hips forward to stand fully upright.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the hamstrings stretching deeper than they ever do on an RDL — that's the stimulus.
commonMistakes: Bending the knees too much: turns it into a deadlift. Lock them nearly straight.
Rounding the back at the bottom: stop earlier, raise the bar with blocks if needed.
Going too heavy: this exercise demands more mobility than strength.
tips: Use lighter loads than your RDL — the deeper range is harder.
Best for intermediate lifters with solid hip mobility.

exercises.name: Barbell Hip Thrust
exercises.cue: Shoulders on bench; bar over hips with pad; full lockout, ribs down.
exercises.description: The best glute-builder in the gym. You sit on the floor with your upper back against a bench, place a loaded barbell across your hips, and drive your hips up to a fully locked-out bridge. The glutes get peak contraction at the top, which is where they grow.
steps: Sit on the floor with your upper back against a bench, knees bent and feet flat.
Roll a loaded barbell over your legs until it sits across your hips — use a pad.
Plant feet hip-width apart, slightly forward of your knees.
Tuck your chin and brace your core.
Drive through your heels to lift the hips up until your body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders.
Squeeze the glutes hard at the top for a 1-second count.
Lower under control back to the floor and reset for the next rep.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: At the top, feel like you're trying to crack a walnut between your butt cheeks — full glute squeeze.
commonMistakes: Not reaching full hip extension: shortchanges the glute squeeze. Lock out fully.
Overarching the lower back at the top: turns the lift into a low-back move. Tuck the ribs.
Feet too close: turns it into a quad lift. Plant them further out.
tips: Use a thick pad or a folded towel — barbells on bare hip bones are brutal.
Many Indian gyms have a Smith machine but no hip thrust bench — Smith machine hip thrusts work great.

exercises.name: Glute Bridge
exercises.cue: Floor version of hip thrust; bridge to full lockout, pause at top.
exercises.description: A simpler version of the hip thrust done flat on the floor. Same idea — drive your hips up to a locked-out bridge — but without the bench, the range of motion is smaller. Great starting point for learning hip-driven glute work before progressing to thrusts.
steps: Lie on the floor with knees bent and feet flat, hip-width apart.
Place a barbell across your hips if loading, or just go bodyweight.
Brace your core and tuck your chin.
Drive through your heels to lift your hips off the floor.
Squeeze the glutes hard at the top, hips fully extended.
Lower under control back to the floor.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Push the floor away with your heels and squeeze the glutes like you're holding a coin between them.
commonMistakes: Hyperextending the lower back: tuck the ribs and pelvis.
Pushing through the toes: pushes work onto quads. Drive through heels.
Half reps: skip the squeeze. Fully extend the hips.
tips: Start with bodyweight, add a barbell once you can do 20 strict reps.
Use a folded towel or pad if the bar bothers your hips.

exercises.name: Cable Pull-Through
exercises.cue: Cable between legs; hinge back, lock out hips with glutes.
exercises.description: A hip-hinge done at the cable station. You stand facing away from a low pulley, run a rope between your legs, and stand up by extending the hips against the cable. Trains the same pattern as RDLs but with constant tension and less spinal load.
steps: Set a cable pulley to the lowest setting with a rope attachment.
Stand facing away from the stack, feet hip-width apart, far enough back to load the cable.
Reach between your legs and grip the rope with both hands.
Hinge at the hips, letting the cable pull the rope back between your legs.
Keep a soft knee bend and a flat back.
Drive your hips forward to stand back up, squeezing the glutes at lockout.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the glutes punching forward at the top, finishing the lift — not the back.
commonMistakes: Squatting instead of hinging: bends knees too much. Keep the knee bend locked.
Standing too close to the stack: kills the load. Step out further.
Pulling with the arms: keeps tension on the back, not glutes. Let arms be hooks.
tips: Great alternative to RDLs on days your lower back is tired.
Pause at the top with the glutes fully squeezed for a 1-second count.

exercises.name: Cable Glute Kickback
exercises.cue: Ankle strap; kick straight back, squeeze; don't arch the low back.
exercises.description: A glute isolation done at the cable station with an ankle strap. You stand facing the stack and kick one leg straight back, squeezing the glute at the top. Trains the glute in isolation, which is rare and useful for shaping work.
steps: Attach an ankle strap to a low cable pulley and clip it to your ankle.
Face the stack and grip the frame for balance.
Slight forward lean at the hips.
Kick the strapped leg straight back, keeping it nearly straight.
Squeeze the glute hard at the back position.
Return slowly under control. Finish all reps before switching legs.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the glute lifting the leg back — not the lower back arching.
commonMistakes: Arching the lower back to swing the leg higher: kills the glute focus. Stay locked.
Bending the knee a lot: shifts work to the hamstring. Keep leg nearly straight.
Going too heavy: ruins the squeeze. Stay light.
tips: Best as a finisher — go light, chase the squeeze, 12–15 reps per side.
Pause at the top for 1 second each rep for extra burn.

exercises.name: Sumo Deadlift
exercises.cue: Wide stance, hands inside; vertical torso; drive knees out hard.
exercises.description: A deadlift done with a wide stance and hands gripping inside the legs. The wide stance shortens the lift's range of motion and pulls in more glutes and quads than a conventional deadlift. Many lifters find sumo friendlier on the lower back.
steps: Stand with feet much wider than shoulder-width, toes turned out about 30 degrees.
Bar over mid-foot, almost touching the shins.
Hinge down and grip the bar inside your legs with palms down.
Pull yourself down and lock chest up, hips lower than in a conventional deadlift.
Brace hard, drive knees out, and push the floor away.
Stand up to a fully locked-out position, squeezing glutes at the top.
Reverse to lower the bar back to the floor.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the glutes powering the hips through to the top — knees drive out, hips drive forward.
commonMistakes: Knees caving in: weakens the lift. Push them out hard.
Lifting with the back instead of legs: drop weight, retrain.
Stance too narrow: turns it into a conventional deadlift. Go wide.
tips: Try both sumo and conventional for a month each — pick the one that feels stronger and friendlier.
Wear flat shoes — no thick soles for stability and stance width.

exercises.name: Reverse Lunge
exercises.cue: Step back; drop into lunge; less knee stress than walking lunges.
exercises.description: A lunge done by stepping backward instead of forward. The reverse step keeps your front knee from drifting too far past your toes, which makes reverse lunges easier on the knees than walking lunges. Glute-dominant when done with an upright torso.
steps: Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand, arms at your sides.
Step one foot back a long stride, planting the ball of the foot.
Lower yourself by bending both knees, dropping the back knee toward the floor.
Stop just before the back knee touches the floor.
Drive up through the front heel to return to standing.
Alternate legs or finish all reps on one side.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the front-leg glute and quad doing the work — back leg is just a balance hook.
commonMistakes: Front knee too far forward: take a longer step back.
Slamming the back knee down: tap lightly.
Torso leaning forward: stay upright.
tips: Stepping back lets you stay in one spot — great for gyms with limited floor space.
Slow the descent for 3 seconds for extra glute and quad work.

exercises.name: Hip Abduction (Machine)
exercises.cue: Lean slightly forward to bias glute med; pause at full abduction.
exercises.description: A seated machine where you push your knees outward against pads. Targets the side glutes (gluteus medius), which give the hip its rounded outer shape. Big squats and deadlifts won't hit this part of the glute the way the abduction machine does.
steps: Sit on the machine with your back against the pad.
Place your knees against the inside of the pads, knees bent.
Grip the side handles and brace your core.
For glute medius bias, lean slightly forward at the hips.
Push the knees outward against the pads as far as comfortable.
Pause and squeeze at the fully open position, then return slowly.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the side of your hip working — the muscle you can poke just behind your hip bone.
commonMistakes: Leaning back: shifts work off the glute medius. Lean slightly forward.
Slamming the stack on return: control the negative.
Half reps: glutes need full ROM. Push wide.
tips: Try a slow 3-second eccentric on the last set for serious side-glute burn.
Pair with hip thrusts on glute day — thrusts hit the bulk, abductions hit the shape.

exercises.name: Standing Calf Raise
exercises.cue: Full stretch at bottom; pause at top; no bouncing.
exercises.description: The standard calf builder. Standing on a step or machine with the balls of your feet, you raise up onto your toes and lower under control. The standing position with straight legs targets the gastrocnemius, the visible 'diamond' part of the calf.
steps: Step onto the calf raise machine with shoulder pads on your shoulders.
Place the balls of your feet on the edge of the platform with heels hanging off.
Stand up so the pads load your shoulders.
Let your heels drop below the platform for a deep stretch.
Push up onto the balls of your feet, rising as high as possible.
Pause at the top for a 1-second squeeze, then lower slowly back to a full stretch.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the calves stretching like rubber bands at the bottom and balling up tight at the top.
commonMistakes: Bouncing at the bottom: lose tension, gain injury risk. Pause briefly.
Half reps: skip the stretch. Heels must drop below the platform.
Going too heavy: ruins ROM. Stay moderate and pause at top and bottom.
tips: Calves respond to extreme volume — 15–20 reps per set, 4+ sets a week.
Hold the top contraction for 2 seconds on the last few reps for extra burn.

exercises.name: Seated Calf Raise
exercises.cue: Knees bent isolates the soleus; slow tempo, deep stretch.
exercises.description: A calf raise done seated with knees bent. The bent-knee position takes the gastrocnemius (upper calf) out of the lift and isolates the soleus — the deeper calf muscle that adds calf thickness when developed. Most people skip this and miss out on a fuller-looking calf.
steps: Sit at the seated calf machine with knees bent at 90 degrees.
Place the balls of your feet on the platform with heels hanging off.
Adjust the thigh pad to lock down firmly across your thighs just above the knees.
Release the safety and let your heels drop below the platform for a stretch.
Push up onto the balls of your feet as high as possible.
Pause and squeeze at the top, then lower slowly back to the stretch.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the deeper part of the calf (behind the shin) doing the work — different feel than standing raises.
commonMistakes: Half reps: skip the stretch. Drop the heels fully.
Bouncing: lose tension. Pause at bottom and top.
Pad too loose: it should pin the thighs firmly.
tips: Lift slow, lower even slower — calves love long time under tension.
Do these every leg day along with standing raises for a complete calf workout.

exercises.name: Leg Press Calf Raise
exercises.cue: Balls of feet on platform edge; full ROM; safer than freestanding loaded.
exercises.description: A calf raise done at the leg press machine. Place the balls of your feet at the bottom edge of the platform and push the platform up by extending the ankles. Lets you handle very heavy loads safely since the machine catches the weight if you fail.
steps: Set up at a leg press as if you're going to do a normal rep.
Place the balls of your feet at the bottom edge of the platform.
Press the platform up to almost-locked legs (keep knees slightly bent).
Release the safety latches.
Let your toes point up so your heels drop and you feel a deep calf stretch.
Press the platform back up by extending the ankles fully.
Pause at the top, then lower slowly.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the calves stretching long at the bottom and balling up like a fist at the top.
commonMistakes: Bending the knees during the lift: turns it into a partial leg press. Keep knees fixed.
Half reps: skip the stretch. Let heels drop fully.
Feet too high on platform: foot slips off the edge. Place at the bottom edge.
tips: Great alternative when the dedicated calf machines are taken.
Use a paused rep style — pause at the top for 2 seconds, then slow lower.

exercises.name: Donkey Calf Raise
exercises.cue: Hinge forward; partner or band on hips; strong stretch position.
exercises.description: An old-school calf raise done hinged forward at the hips, with weight on your hips from either a partner sitting on you or a heavy band. The forward lean puts the calves in a deeper stretch than upright raises and adds intensity. Rare to see, but extremely effective.
steps: Stand on a raised platform with the balls of your feet on the edge.
Bend forward at the hips and brace yourself on a bench or rail.
Have a partner sit on your lower back/hips, or loop a heavy band across your hips.
Let your heels drop below the platform for a deep stretch.
Push up onto the balls of your feet as high as possible.
Pause at the top, squeeze the calves, then lower slowly.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the calves stretching deeper than usual because of the forward hip hinge.
commonMistakes: Bending the knees during the lift: kills the calf isolation. Keep them straight.
Rushing the rep: trains nothing. Slow tempo.
Half reps: skip the stretch. Heels must drop fully.
tips: If no partner is around, use a sturdy band looped under your feet over your hips.
Few Indian gyms have a donkey calf machine — improvise with a smith machine and lean forward against the bar.

exercises.name: Single-Leg Calf Raise
exercises.cue: One leg, full stretch; great for unilateral imbalance work.
exercises.description: A calf raise done on one leg at a time, usually on a step or platform. Each side works independently, which fixes left-right calf imbalances and lets you push closer to failure than two-leg raises since the load is concentrated on one calf.
steps: Stand on a step or platform with the ball of one foot on the edge.
Hold a rail or wall for balance.
Lift the other leg off the platform behind you.
Let your heel drop below the platform for a full stretch.
Push up onto the ball of your foot as high as possible.
Pause at the top, then lower slowly. Finish all reps on one side before switching.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel one calf doing all the work — the load is now twice as concentrated.
commonMistakes: Pushing off the other foot: defeats single-leg training. Keep it lifted.
Half reps: stretch is everything. Drop heel fully.
Going too fast: trains nothing. Slow tempo.
tips: Add a dumbbell in your free hand once bodyweight feels easy.
Aim for 15+ reps per side — calves love volume.

exercises.name: Hanging Leg Raise
exercises.cue: Dead hang; raise straight legs to parallel or higher; no swing.
exercises.description: Hanging from a pull-up bar, you raise your straight legs in front of you to at least parallel with the floor. Hits the entire abs section, especially the lower abs, while also building strong grip and shoulder stability.
steps: Hang from a pull-up bar with palms facing away, shoulder-width grip.
Pull your shoulder blades down and engage the lats slightly.
Brace your core.
Raise both legs together in front of you, keeping them straight.
Continue until legs are parallel with the floor or higher.
Lower slowly under control. No swinging — pause if needed at the bottom.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the lower abs curling the hips up toward the ribs — not just lifting the legs.
commonMistakes: Swinging the legs: trains momentum. Pause at the bottom of every rep.
Bending the knees a lot: makes it easier. Keep legs straight for max difficulty.
Not curling the pelvis: lifts only with hip flexors. Tilt the pelvis up at the top.
tips: If straight legs are too hard, start with bent-knee raises and progress over time.
Use straps if grip fails before the core does.

exercises.name: Cable Crunch
exercises.cue: Kneel; rope behind head; crunch by rounding spine, hips don't move.
exercises.description: A loaded ab crunch done kneeling at a cable station. The cable provides resistance you can scale up, which lets the abs grow stronger — most bodyweight ab work tops out before the abs are fully challenged. The crunch is in the spine, not the hips.
steps: Set a cable pulley to the highest position and attach a rope.
Kneel facing the stack with the rope ends gripped on either side of your head.
Brace the core and hinge slightly forward at the hips to load the cable.
Crunch down by rounding your upper back toward your hips — like curling forward.
Hips stay still — the crunch is in the spine, not the hip joint.
Squeeze the abs hard at the bottom, then return slowly to the start.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the abs pulling your ribcage toward your hips — round the spine, don't bend at the hips.
commonMistakes: Hinging at the hips instead of rounding the spine: turns it into a hip flexor move. Round the back.
Pulling the rope down with the arms: trains lats. Lock arms and use abs.
Going too heavy: defeats the crunch. Stay moderate to feel the abs.
tips: Hold the bottom contraction for 1 second on each rep for extra ab burn.
Pair with leg raises for a complete abs workout — crunches hit upper abs, leg raises hit lower.

exercises.name: Ab Wheel Rollout
exercises.cue: Roll out as far as you can hold neutral spine; pull yourself back.
exercises.description: Kneeling on the floor, you roll an ab wheel forward as far as you can while keeping your back flat, then pull yourself back. One of the hardest and most effective ab exercises — the abs fight to keep your spine from sagging.
steps: Kneel on a mat with the ab wheel on the floor in front of you.
Grip the handles with both hands, arms straight.
Brace your core hard and squeeze your glutes.
Roll the wheel forward, letting your body extend out toward the floor.
Stop just before your back starts to sag — that's your current limit.
Pull the wheel back to the start by contracting the abs hard.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the abs fighting like crazy to keep your back from sagging — that fight is the exercise.
commonMistakes: Sagging hips: turns into a back exercise and risks low-back injury. Maintain a tight line.
Rolling out too far too soon: builds up over weeks, not days. Stop short.
Standing rollouts before kneeling are mastered: stay on knees for months first.
tips: Use a band looped around the wheel and a sturdy upright behind you for an assisted version while learning.
Most Indian gyms don't have an ab wheel — bring your own or use a barbell with small plates on each side.

exercises.name: Plank
exercises.cue: Straight line head to heels; squeeze glutes; quality > duration.
exercises.description: An isometric hold where you support yourself on forearms and toes with your body in a perfectly straight line. The abs and lower back work hard to hold position. Best for building endurance and bracing skill, not for growth — but excellent for core stability.
steps: Lie face down and rest on your forearms with elbows under your shoulders.
Extend your legs back so just your toes are on the floor.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes.
Form a straight line from your heels to your head.
Hold the position — breathe steadily through clenched abs.
Stop when you can't hold the perfect line, not when it gets uncomfortable.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel your whole front side — abs, hip flexors, quads — holding the body rigid like a steel plank.
commonMistakes: Sagging hips: kills the exercise. Squeeze glutes harder.
Hips piked up: cheats the core. Lower into a straight line.
Holding for hours: low value past 60 seconds. Make it harder, don't hold longer.
tips: Once you can hold 60 seconds, progress to harder variations like RKC plank, side plank, or weighted plank.
Plank is a warmup, not a workout — pair with cable crunches or leg raises for ab growth.

exercises.name: Pallof Press
exercises.cue: Cable at chest height; press out, resist rotation; underrated anti-rotation.
exercises.description: An anti-rotation core exercise done at the cable station. You stand sideways to a cable at chest height, press a handle straight out in front of you, and fight the cable's pull trying to twist your torso. Builds rock-solid rotational stability — useful for everything from squats to running.
steps: Set a cable pulley to chest height with a single handle.
Stand sideways to the stack, far enough away to load the cable.
Grip the handle with both hands at your chest.
Brace your core hard.
Press the handle straight out in front of you to arms-length.
Hold for 2 seconds, fighting the cable's pull. Return slowly to your chest and repeat.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the obliques and abs cranking on hard to keep your torso from twisting sideways.
commonMistakes: Letting the torso twist: defeats the exercise. Lock the hips and shoulders square.
Going too heavy: forces you to twist. Drop the weight.
Standing too close to the stack: kills the load. Step out further.
tips: Underrated core exercise — most people do crunches when they should be doing Pallof presses.
Add a slow press-and-hold for 5 seconds per rep on the last set.

exercises.name: Dead Bug
exercises.cue: Low back pressed to floor; opposite arm and leg extend slowly.
exercises.description: Lying on your back, you slowly extend opposite arm and leg while keeping your low back pressed firmly to the floor. Trains the deep core muscles that protect the spine. Looks easy, harder than it looks when done correctly.
steps: Lie on your back, arms straight up over your shoulders.
Bend your hips and knees to 90 degrees, shins parallel with the floor.
Press your lower back firmly against the floor — no gap.
Slowly lower one arm overhead and the opposite leg toward the floor.
Stop just before your lower back lifts off the floor.
Return to start, then switch sides.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the deep abs pressing your spine into the floor — that's the work, not the arm and leg motion.
commonMistakes: Letting the lower back arch: defeats the exercise. Press it down hard.
Going too fast: kills the bracing. Slow, controlled reps.
Holding breath: breathe through your braced core.
tips: Great warmup for any heavy lower-body day — trains the bracing pattern you need under load.
Add a band around your hands and feet for extra core challenge once basic version feels easy.

exercises.name: Weighted Sit-Up
exercises.cue: Hold plate at chest; full sit-up; protect the neck.
exercises.description: A sit-up done while holding a weight plate against your chest. Adding load is what turns sit-ups from an endurance move into a growth exercise. Easy to set up and effective when done with strict form.
steps: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat.
Anchor your feet under something heavy or have a partner hold them.
Hold a weight plate against your chest with both hands.
Sit up by curling your upper body toward your knees.
Continue until your torso is roughly vertical.
Lower slowly back to the floor under control.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the abs pulling your ribcage up toward your hips — that curl is the lift.
commonMistakes: Yanking on the neck: avoid. Hold the plate to the chest, not behind the head.
Hip flexors taking over: focus on curling the spine, not just hinging at the hips.
Half reps: shortchanges the abs. Sit fully up.
tips: Start with 5 kg and add 2.5 kg every 2 weeks as it gets easier.
Slow the descent for 3 seconds for extra ab work.

exercises.name: Hollow Body Hold
exercises.cue: Lower back glued to floor; arms and legs off ground; gymnastic staple.
exercises.description: A gymnastics-style ab hold. Lying on your back, you press the lower back into the floor and lift the arms and legs off the floor at the same time — creating a long, banana-shape body. Brutal on the entire ab section.
steps: Lie on your back with legs straight and arms overhead.
Press your lower back firmly into the floor.
Brace your core and lift your shoulders, head, arms, and legs a few inches off the floor.
Hold the position — body forms a slight curve, low back never leaves the floor.
Breathe through the brace.
Hold for time — quality of position matters more than duration.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the whole front of the core working overtime to keep the lower back glued to the floor.
commonMistakes: Lower back peeling off the floor: defeats the move. Lower the legs slightly until the back stays flat.
Holding breath: breathe steadily through the brace.
Holding too long with bad form: stop when the back lifts.
tips: Start with 10-second holds and build up to 45 seconds with perfect form.
Bend the knees if straight legs cause the back to lift — progression over perfection.

exercises.name: Captain's Chair Knee Raise
exercises.cue: Forearms on pads; lift knees toward chest; no swinging.
exercises.description: An ab exercise done on a captain's chair — a frame with arm pads where you support yourself on your forearms with your legs hanging. You raise your knees toward your chest using just the lower abs. Easier than hanging leg raises while still hitting the same lower-ab pattern.
steps: Step into the captain's chair and place your forearms on the pads, gripping the handles.
Press your back firmly against the back pad.
Let your legs hang straight down, feet off the floor.
Brace your core.
Raise your knees up toward your chest by curling the lower back slightly.
Pause at the top, then lower slowly. No swing — pause at the bottom if needed.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the lower abs curling the pelvis up toward the ribcage — knees come up because the pelvis tilts.
commonMistakes: Swinging the legs: trains momentum. Pause at the bottom.
Not curling the pelvis: trains only hip flexors. Tilt the pelvis up at the top.
Half reps: bring knees to chest, not just to parallel.
tips: Most Indian gyms have this combined into the assisted pull-up/dip machine — just step off the assistance pad and use the forearm rests.
Progress to straight-leg raises and then hanging leg raises as you get stronger.

exercises.name: Barbell Wrist Curl
exercises.cue: Forearms on bench, wrists hanging off; curl bar with the wrist only.
exercises.description: A small isolation move where you rest your forearms on a bench with your wrists hanging off the edge, then curl a barbell up using only the wrists. Targets the forearm flexors directly — the muscles that close your hand and curl the wrist.
steps: Sit on a bench with a barbell loaded light.
Place your forearms flat on your thighs or a bench with palms facing up.
Let your wrists hang off the edge with the barbell in your hands.
Let the bar roll down to your fingertips.
Curl the bar back up by closing the hand and flexing the wrist.
Pause at the top, then lower slowly.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the muscles on the inside of your forearm pumping as the wrist curls up.
commonMistakes: Lifting the forearms off the bench: defeats the isolation. Pin them.
Going too heavy: forearms are smaller than you think. Start light.
Skipping the fingertip roll: lose the full forearm activation. Let the bar roll down.
tips: Train forearms after the bigger lifts — they get worked indirectly by everything else first.
High reps work well — try sets of 15–20.

exercises.name: Barbell Reverse Wrist Curl
exercises.cue: Same setup, palms down; lighter load, longer ROM, hits extensors.
exercises.description: Same setup as a wrist curl, but with palms facing down instead of up. Targets the forearm extensors — the muscles that open the hand and extend the wrist. Most people have weak extensors compared to flexors, so reverse curls balance the forearm out.
steps: Sit on a bench with a light barbell.
Rest your forearms on your thighs with palms facing down.
Let your wrists hang off your knees with the barbell in your hands.
Let the bar drop down toward the floor as far as your wrist allows.
Curl the bar back up by extending the wrist (lifting the back of your hand).
Pause at the top, then lower slowly.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the top of the forearm working — the muscles that run along the back of your arm.
commonMistakes: Going too heavy: extensors are much weaker than flexors. Use about half the load.
Forearms lifting off the thighs: defeats the isolation. Pin them.
Short ROM: skip the stretch. Drop the bar fully.
tips: Use about 50% of your normal wrist curl weight — extensors are smaller and weaker.
Helps prevent tennis elbow if you do a lot of curls or pull-ups.

exercises.name: EZ-Bar Reverse Curl
exercises.cue: Overhand grip on EZ-bar; curl as normal; hammers the brachioradialis.
exercises.description: A biceps curl done with an overhand grip on an EZ-bar. The overhand grip shifts most of the work onto the brachioradialis — the big forearm muscle on the thumb side of your arm. Builds noticeable forearm thickness when other forearm work doesn't.
steps: Grip an EZ-bar with palms facing down, hands at the angled portion of the bar.
Stand with arms hanging at your thighs.
Pin elbows to your sides.
Curl the bar up toward your chest, keeping wrists locked straight.
Squeeze the top of the forearms at the peak.
Lower slowly back to your thighs.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the meaty part on the thumb side of your forearm doing the curling.
commonMistakes: Letting wrists bend: turns it into a wrist curl. Keep them locked straight.
Going too heavy: forearms can't lift what biceps can. Drop the weight.
Body swing: trains momentum. Stay still.
tips: Use about 60% of your normal biceps curl weight.
Pair with regular biceps curls for a complete arm workout — biceps for the peak, reverse curls for the thickness.

exercises.name: Farmer's Carry
exercises.cue: Heavy dumbbells; walk tall; grip and core trainer in one.
exercises.description: Pick up two heavy dumbbells and walk. The grip works overtime to hold the weights, the traps work to keep the shoulders up, and the core works to keep you upright. One of the simplest and most effective full-body conditioning moves.
steps: Grab a heavy dumbbell in each hand and stand tall.
Pull shoulders back and down, chest up.
Brace your core.
Walk forward with short, controlled steps.
Keep the body tall — no leaning or swaying.
Cover a set distance (20–30 meters) or walk for time (30–60 seconds).
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the grip burning, the traps holding the shoulders up, and the core keeping you straight.
commonMistakes: Dumbbells swinging: causes the body to twist. Keep them controlled.
Shoulders hunched: defeats trap work. Stay tall.
Walking too fast: turns it into cardio. Short, deliberate steps.
tips: Use a weight you can carry for about 30 seconds before grip gives out.
Great finisher to any workout — builds grip, traps, and conditioning all at once.

exercises.name: Dead Hang
exercises.cue: Hang from bar; full body relaxed except grip; build hang time.
exercises.description: Hang from a pull-up bar with arms straight. That's it. Builds grip strength and stretches the shoulders. Great preparation for pull-ups and a useful daily habit even on rest days.
steps: Reach up and grip a pull-up bar with palms facing away, shoulder-width.
Hang with arms straight and feet off the floor.
Let the shoulders relax slightly (passive hang) or pull them down (active hang).
Keep the body relaxed except for the grip.
Breathe steadily.
Hold for time — drop when grip gives out, not before.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the forearms locked tight on the bar while the rest of the body hangs loose.
commonMistakes: Letting the shoulders shrug up to the ears: causes shoulder strain. Stay relaxed or actively pull down.
Holding breath: breathe steady.
Kicking and swinging: stay still.
tips: Aim to build to 60+ seconds of hang time — that's solid grip for most people.
Add load with a dip belt once 90 seconds is easy.

exercises.name: Plate Pinch
exercises.cue: Pinch two plates smooth-side-out; hold for time.
exercises.description: Pinch two plates together with one hand, smooth sides out, and hold them up for time. Trains the pinch grip — a different grip strength than holding a bar. Niche but useful for strongman-style training or unique grip challenges.
steps: Set two weight plates on the floor with the smooth sides facing out.
Squat down and pinch them together between your thumb and fingers.
Stand up, holding the plates at your side.
Keep the body tall — no leaning.
Hold for time, switch hands, repeat.
Drop the plates when grip gives out.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the muscle between your thumb and fingers cranking on to keep the plates from slipping.
commonMistakes: Plates too heavy: drops in 5 seconds. Start with two 5 kg plates.
Plates with rough edges: hurts the fingers. Use smooth-sided plates.
Plates uneven: shift the grip. Stack them flat together.
tips: Most Indian gyms have plenty of smooth-sided plates — try two 5 kg or two 10 kg to start.
Niche exercise — skip if grip already gets enough from carries and pulls.

exercises.name: Barbell Shrug
exercises.cue: Heavy bar (use straps); shrug straight up; no rolls.
exercises.description: Holding a heavy barbell in front of your thighs, you shrug your shoulders straight up toward your ears. Simple and brutal trap-builder. Most people undertrain traps because shrugs feel basic — but they respond fast to heavy loads.
steps: Stand with feet shoulder-width, gripping a barbell at thigh level with palms facing your body.
Stand tall, chest up, arms straight.
Brace your core.
Shrug your shoulders straight up toward your ears as high as possible.
Pause and squeeze at the top.
Lower slowly back to the starting position.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Imagine touching your ears with your shoulders — straight up, no roll, just shrug.
commonMistakes: Rolling the shoulders: useless for traps and stresses the joint. Shrug straight up.
Half reps: skip the squeeze. Go as high as possible.
Bending elbows: trains biceps. Keep arms straight.
tips: Use straps as soon as the load gets heavy — your grip will fail before traps.
Pause at the top for 1–2 seconds to maximize the trap squeeze.

exercises.name: Dumbbell Shrug
exercises.cue: Dumbbells at sides; shrug high, hold a count, control down.
exercises.description: A shrug done with a dumbbell in each hand instead of a barbell. The dumbbells hang at your sides instead of in front, which gives a slightly different angle of pull on the traps. Often more comfortable than barbell shrugs for taller lifters.
steps: Stand with a dumbbell in each hand, arms at your sides.
Stand tall, chest up, shoulders pulled back.
Brace your core.
Shrug your shoulders straight up toward your ears.
Pause and squeeze at the top.
Lower slowly back down to your sides.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the traps balling up tight at the top — like trying to crush a walnut between shoulder and ear.
commonMistakes: Rolling the shoulders forward or back: shrug straight up.
Going too heavy and using body swing: drop the weight.
Half reps: lift as high as possible for full trap activation.
tips: Most Indian gym dumbbells max out at 40–50 kg — once you outgrow them, switch to barbell shrugs.
Use a slow 3-second lower for extra time under tension.

exercises.name: Rack Pull
exercises.cue: Bar set just below knees; partial deadlift overload for upper back.
exercises.description: A partial deadlift done with the bar set on rack pins just below the knees. The shorter range of motion lets you load heavier than a full deadlift, which overloads the upper back and traps. Great for building back thickness when full deadlifts get too taxing.
steps: Set the safety pins of a rack just below knee height.
Load a barbell on the pins.
Set up like a deadlift with the bar over mid-foot, hands just outside the legs.
Pull yourself down to the bar with a flat back, chest up.
Brace hard and pull the bar straight up by extending the hips and pulling the shoulders back.
Stand fully upright, then lower the bar back to the pins.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the upper back and traps cranking the shoulders back as the bar locks out at the top.
commonMistakes: Rounding the back: stop and reset. Stay flat.
Bouncing the bar off the pins: defeats the dead start. Pause for a beat.
Pin height too low: turns it into a regular deadlift. Set just below knees.
tips: You can usually rack pull 30–40% more than your deadlift — use straps once load gets heavy.
Great alternative on a back day when you don't want to do a full deadlift.

exercises.name: Snatch-Grip High Pull
exercises.cue: Wide grip; explosive hip drive; bar to upper chest, elbows high.
exercises.description: An explosive pull from the floor with a very wide (snatch) grip, finishing with the bar pulled to your upper chest. Combines a deadlift, shrug, and upright row into one explosive movement. Builds traps, back, and athleticism all at once.
steps: Stand over a barbell with feet hip-width, bar over mid-foot.
Grip the bar very wide — almost to the plates (snatch grip).
Set up like a deadlift with chest up and flat back.
Pull the bar off the floor by pushing the floor away.
As the bar passes the knees, explode upward with the hips.
Pull the bar up to your upper chest, leading with the elbows.
Lower the bar back to the floor and reset.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the whole back of the body — hamstrings, glutes, back, traps — firing in a single explosive chain.
commonMistakes: Curling the bar with the arms: kills the explosive pull. Drive with the hips.
Slow pull: defeats the purpose. The movement is explosive.
Wide grip stresses the wrists too much: drop the weight or narrow the grip slightly.
tips: Best for intermediate to advanced lifters with good form on deadlifts.
Use straps once load gets heavy — wide grip is hard to hold.

exercises.name: Cable Shrug
exercises.cue: Cable from below; shrug up and slightly back; constant tension.
exercises.description: A shrug done at the cable station with the pulley set low. The cable provides constant tension throughout the shrug, where dumbbells and barbells lose tension at the top. Great variation when traps need a fresh stimulus.
steps: Set a cable pulley to the lowest setting with a straight bar or rope attachment.
Stand facing the stack, grip the attachment with both hands.
Step back to load the cable, arms straight at thigh level.
Stand tall, chest up.
Shrug straight up toward your ears, pulling slightly back at the top.
Pause and squeeze, then lower slowly back to the start.
exercises.mindMuscleCue: Feel the traps under constant pull through the whole rep — never a moment of rest.
commonMistakes: Rolling the shoulders: shrug straight up.
Standing too close to the stack: kills the tension at the bottom. Step back.
Rushing the negative: control the lower for extra time under tension.
tips: Great finisher after heavier shrugs — go light, chase the pump.
Try with a rope attachment for a bit more grip variety.
